sens: Number equal to five times one thousand units
Large crowd gathered in one place
G4000.detail:
1. The word literally means the number 5,000, formed from "penta" (five) and "chilioi" (thousand). It is a precise figure in the Greek numbering system, used here to count exactly the people present.
2. In all biblical uses, this number refers to the crowd of people that Jesus miraculously fed: "Those who had eaten the loaves were five thousand men" (Mark 6:44). The word evokes less an abstract sum than a concrete multitude, a massive assembly sitting on the grass and receiving food.
G4000.origine: The word combines two Greek elements: "penta" (five, scholarly element) and "chilioi" (thousand). The formation into a single compound adjective shows that the Greek of the New Testament borrows terms that combine several numerical elements to express large numbers with precision. The structure recalls how Hebrew and ancient Greek assembled units to name quantities beyond a thousand.
G4000.emploi: This word appears only six times in the New Testament, always to refer to a single event reported by four evangelists: the feeding of the five thousand. Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John all mention "five thousand men" as the crowd fed by Jesus. Matthew revisits this number twice: first when recounting the miracle (14:21), and a second time when Jesus reminds his disciples of this event to encourage them not to fear lack (16:9). Mark does the same (6:44 and 8:19). Luke and John mention it only once each (9:14 and 6:10). The number is given as "about" by Luke and John, while Matthew and Mark state it more directly. This shows that the precise figure matters less than the certainty that Jesus fed an impressive crowd.
G4000.portee: This number reminds us that Jesus' care for the hungry crowd is not a marginal or isolated act: it is a miracle performed before thousands of witnesses. For the ancient reader, "five thousand" was not an abstraction, but the image of an enormous assembly, almost impossible to feed without divine help. This account, repeated and meditated upon in the early Church, invites every Christian to recognize that Jesus truly provides for the needs of the crowds that gather around him, and that entrusting him with our shortcomings, even when they seem enormous, is to enter into his logic of compassion and abundance.

sens: The number 500
G4001.detail: 1. It is the number five hundred, used to quantify people or things. Luke mentions a debtor who owed five hundred denarii (Luke 7:41), which is a very large sum of money — much more than the one who owed fifty. Paul recalls that the risen Christ appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once (1 Corinthians 15:6), emphasizing the importance of the number of witnesses to the Resurrection.
G4001.origine: The word comes from the composition of two Greek roots: penta (five) and kosioi (hundreds). It is a regular compound number in Greek, formed like other hundreds by associating the unit digit with the order of hundreds.
G4001.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In the parable of the unforgiving servant (Luke 7:41), it serves to dramatize the comparison between two debts: five hundred denarii versus fifty, to show the absurdity of one who refuses to forgive a small debt after having received the cancellation of a huge one. In 1 Corinthians 15:6, Paul uses this number to attest to the reliability of the Resurrection: many witnesses still alive at the time of writing can confirm that they saw the risen Lord.
G4001.portee: These two passages teach the transformative power of limitless forgiveness, on one hand, and the historical solidity of apostolic testimony to the Resurrection on the other. The large number of witnesses makes faith in the Resurrection based on established facts, not on rumors.

sens: the number 5
a small quantity of food or goods
a measured period of time
a collection or group of five elements
a monetary value
G4002.detail:
1. Five is the number that comes after four: it is a simple, concrete figure. It often appears in the accounts of Jesus' miracles, particularly when he multiplies the bread — "We have here only five loaves and two fish" (Matthew 14:17).
2. When the Bible speaks of five loaves or five talents, this small number emphasizes the modesty of the means: it is little, but it is what we have. In the parable, the one who received five talents puts them to work and gains five more (Matthew 25:16).
3. For time, five can refer to months (Elizabeth "hid herself for five months," Luke 1:24) or a unit of days.
4. Five is also used to count a collection: five pairs of oxen, five gates (John 5:2), five virgins (Matthew 25:2).
5. In Acts 19:19, the value of the burned books of magic amounts to fifty thousand pieces of silver — here the word "piece" translates a form of five, expressing a significant sum.
G4002.origine: Πέντε comes from ancient Greek, with no visible morphological relation to other numbers, like many small numbers in Greek and Hebrew. It is a root word, a base of the Greek numbering system. Hebrew uses חָמֵשׁ (hamesh) for "five," and the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament) systematically uses πέντε to translate it.
G4002.emploi: The number five appears 33 times in the New Testament provided here. It is particularly frequent in Matthew and Luke, in miracle accounts and parables. In the miracles of the multiplication of loaves (Matthew 14:17, Mark 6:38, John 6:9), the number five recurs regularly. The parable of the talents (Matthew 25) uses it to enumerate the gifts distributed. Luke uses it to count time (Luke 1:24) or family divisions (Luke 12:52). In Revelation, five takes on a symbolic coloring: the locusts torment for five months (Revelation 9:5). The word can also denote a monetary value (Acts 19:19).
G4002.portee: For the believer, this small number reminds us that God never despises modest resources — five loaves and two fish fed a crowd. It invites us to put into God's service what we have, however little it may be, in trust. The parable of the talents teaches that everyone receives a measure and must use it faithfully.

sens: which occupies the rank number fifteen in an ordered series
which marks or counts the division by fifteen
G4003.detail:
1. This word designates what comes in the fifteenth position in an order or succession. In the Gospel of Luke, it applies to the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius, the Roman emperor (Luke 3:1) — a way to precisely date a historical event by counting the years since the beginning of a reign.
2. More broadly, it can also qualify what is divided or counted according to the number fifteen, although this figurative sense is not present in the preserved biblical uses.
G4003.origine: The Greek word is composed of three elements: "pente" (five), "kai" (and), and "dekatos" (tenth). Literally, it means "five-and-tenth," that is, fifteen. It is an ordinal number, which classifies and orders, rather than simply counting. Greek forms its ordinals (the words that denote rank: first, second, etc.) by adding suffixes to cardinal numbers (five, ten, etc.).
G4003.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:1. The evangelist uses it to establish the moment when John the Baptist begins his ministry in relation to the political power of Rome: "the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar." This choice of chronological precision anchors the event in real and verifiable history, showing that the facts reported by the Gospel are situated in a concrete and dated historical context.
G4003.portee: This word reminds us that the Gospel is not a timeless legend, but the irruption of God into real human history, at a specific time and place. The mention of the fifteenth year of the reign of a pagan emperor invites the reader to see how God acts in the world of the powerful of this world and how his word is fulfilled independently of their will.

sens: the number 50
arrangement or grouping in sets of 50
G4004.detail:
1. Fifty is simply the number 50. It appears in very concrete situations: a debt of fifty denarii (Luke 7:41), the approximate age of Jesus estimated by his opponents (John 8:57), or the exact number of one hundred fifty-three fish in Peter's net (John 21:11).
2. The word is also used to indicate how to arrange or group people. Jesus tells his disciples to have the crowds sit down "in groups of fifty" (Luke 9:14), an organization that allows everyone to be fed in an orderly manner. Mark reports the same scene with the same arrangement: "in groups of hundreds and fifties" (Mark 6:40).
G4004.origine: The Greek word πεντήκοντα comes from the root "pente" which means five. Fifty is five times ten: it is a natural compound of these two fundamental numbers. The word is simply the number, without any hidden poetic imagery.
G4004.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the New Testament. Luke uses it most (4 occurrences), particularly to recount how Jesus organizes the crowd during the feeding of the multitude. John uses it twice: for the supposed age of Jesus and for the number of miraculous fish. Mark also recounts the organization by fifty. One occurrence in Acts 13:20 completes this picture. Each time, it is a concrete, specific number, not a mere approximation: Luke emphasizes the numerical details.
G4004.portee: This number invites the reader to notice the order and wisdom of Jesus: he does not leave the crowd in disarray; he organizes them before feeding them. It is also a call to precision: the numbers in the Gospel are not vague; God knows the exact and cares about it.

sens: Jewish feast celebrated fifty days after Passover
Day when the Holy Spirit was given to the disciples of Jesus
G4005.detail:
1. Pentecost is a major traditional Jewish feast, the second of the three solemn feasts of the people of Israel. Its name comes from the number fifty: it is celebrated exactly fifty days after Passover. It is a harvest and thanksgiving feast for the first fruits of the harvest (Acts 2:1; 20:16).
2. For Christians, Pentecost is especially the memorable day when God poured out His Holy Spirit on the disciples of the risen Jesus and on the early Church (Acts 2:1). On that day, the disciples received the power promised by Jesus and began to boldly proclaim the Gospel (1 Corinthians 16:8).
G4005.origine: The Greek word « pentêkostê » literally means « the fiftieth (day) ». It comes from the adjective « pentêkostos » which designates the number fifty. In Hebrew, the feast is called « Chag Shavouot » (Feast of Weeks), as it occurs seven weeks after Passover. Greek-speaking Jews adopted the name « Pentecost » because it recalls this fifty-day interval.
G4005.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always to refer to this Jewish feast or the time when it occurs. In Acts 2:1, Pentecost is the setting for the giving of the Holy Spirit to the apostles, the founding event of the Christian Church. In Acts 20:16, Paul desires to arrive in Jerusalem for Pentecost, showing that Christians still observed these Jewish feasts. In 1 Corinthians 16:8, Paul indicates that he will remain in Ephesus until Pentecost, using the feast as a temporal marker. Thus, Pentecost retains its meaning as an important Jewish religious feast, but it acquires a new and significant meaning for Christians with the giving of the Spirit.
G4005.portee: Pentecost reminds Christians that the Holy Spirit is God's central gift to His Church. It marks the fulfillment of Jesus' promise and the beginning of divine power in the lives of believers. Celebrating or remembering Pentecost is to acknowledge that the Holy Spirit equips us to witness to Jesus Christ and to live the Christian life in power.

sens: State of one who firmly believes in someone or something
Inner assurance, firmness of soul in the face of a situation
Freedom and boldness to act or speak without fear
Personal conviction, intimate persuasion
G4006.detail: 1. Confidence is the state of one who firmly believes in someone or something, and who relies on that certainty. Paul says he has "confidence" in Christ before God (2 Corinthians 3:4): it is the certainty that Christ supports him in his relationship with the Father. 2. It also refers to inner assurance, the firmness of soul in the face of a difficult situation. When Paul speaks of approaching "with confidence" to boldness, he evokes the firmness of one who does not hesitate to use his apostolic authority (2 Corinthians 10:2). 3. It is also the freedom and boldness to act or speak without fear: believers have "the freedom to approach God with confidence" through faith in Jesus (Ephesians 3:12), that is, the respectful boldness to enter the presence of the Father. 4. Finally, it expresses a personal conviction, an intimate persuasion: Paul uses the word when he speaks of his initial "confidence" in going to see the Corinthians (2 Corinthians 1:15), and when he says he has reason to put his confidence in fleshly advantages (Philippians 3:4).
G4006.origine: The word comes from the verb πείθω (peithô), which means "to persuade" or "to convince". The root evokes the idea of creating in oneself or in others a firm conviction. The Hebrew word בִּטָּחוֹן (bittachôn), "confidence", which the Greek translation of the Old Testament uses to render similar situations, reinforces this idea of security based on certainty.
G4006.emploi: This word appears six times in the New Testament, only in the Pauline epistles (2 Corinthians three times, Ephesians once, Philippians once, and once in 2 Corinthians). Paul uses it to describe the Christian's confidence in God or the Lord Jesus, either as spiritual assurance in the action of God, or as freedom to act or speak. In the letters to the Corinthians, the word also takes on a nuance of apostolic authority: Paul possesses the confidence of his role and the firmness to use it. In Ephesians and Philippians, it is the religious and personal confidence of the believer that predominates.
G4006.portee: This word invites the Christian to understand that true confidence is not mere personal optimism, but a certainty grounded in Christ and God. It frees from fear and allows a respectful yet bold approach to the Father. It is not arrogance, but just assurance, rooted in faith and not in human strengths or merits.

sens: the opposite shore of a body of water (sea, lake, river)
the region located beyond a natural boundary
the sense of movement or passage to that other side
G4008.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the other shore of a body of water. Jesus often crosses the Sea of Galilee with his disciples, and it is said that they pass "to the other side" (Mark 4:35, 5:1). It's simple: there is water, and one goes to the opposite shore.
2. It also applies to entire regions located beyond a river or sea. "Beyond the Jordan" refers to the Transjordan region, meaning the lands east of the Jordan (Matthew 4:15; John 1:28). The water or river serves as a boundary line between two lands.
3. Sometimes the word conveys the idea of the passage itself, the movement going from one side to the other: "He got back into the boat to cross to the other side" (Mark 8:13). The word then encompasses the action of crossing.
G4008.origine: The Greek word πέραν comes from a root meaning "to cross" or "to go beyond." In Hebrew, the idea is found in עֵבֶר ("beyond"), which designates the lands located on the other side of a natural boundary. It is a very concrete word, related to travel and overcoming obstacles.
G4008.emploi: The word appears 23 times in the New Testament, primarily in the Gospels (Matthew 13 times, Mark 9 times, Luke 1 time, John 6 times). Jesus and his disciples regularly cross water: he crosses the Sea of Galilee (Mark 4:35, 5:1, 6:45), he goes beyond the Jordan (Matthew 4:15, 19:1, John 1:28, 10:40), and even crosses the Kidron Valley to go to Gethsemane (John 18:1). The expression "the other side" (without a preposition) becomes almost technical to designate the opposite shore when a group crosses (Matthew 8:18, 14:22, Mark 5:21). The word remains very concrete and geographical: it is never used in a figurative sense in the New Testament.
G4008.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus' movements are not abstract: he travels in reality, he crosses natural obstacles, he goes to meet people. The accounts of the crossings of the lake (calming the storm, healing the demoniac) show Jesus acting in the real world, and his word extends beyond borders: even those who live "on the other side" of the Jordan know him. It is a simple detail that anchors the Gospel in geography and history.

sens: The end, the farthest point of a region or the world
The end, that which brings something to a conclusion
G4009.detail:
1. The extremity is the final point, the end of a region or expanse. It marks the farthest limit, where the territory ends. When the queen of the South comes from the "extremities of the earth" to hear Solomon (Matthew 12:42, Luke 11:31), she comes from the edge of the known world, from very far away. Similarly, the word from the Psalm quoted in Romans 10:18 has gone "to the extremities of the world," meaning to the farthest limits of the inhabited earth.
2. The extremity can also refer to that which brings something to an end, that which completes it. In Hebrews 6:16, the oath is "a guarantee that ends all their disputes": it concludes the conflict, it is what stops and resolves. It is the ultimate term, the one that closes the discussion.
G4009.origine: The Greek word πέρας comes from the root πέρα which means "beyond," "on the other side." This explains why it designates what is far, extreme, at the limits. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), πέρας primarily translates the Hebrew קֵץ (limit, end) and קָצָה (end, extremity) and their related forms. The word expresses the idea of what exceeds, goes to the end, reaches its ultimate limit.
G4009.emploi: The word πέρας appears four times in the New Testament. It is mostly used in the plural to speak of the "extremities of the earth" or the "world" in the Gospels and Paul: it is a geographical term that designates distant regions, the borders of the inhabited world. In Matthew and Luke, the queen of the South comes from the "extremities" to seek wisdom. In Romans, the voice of the Gospel has reached the "extremities of the world." Only once, in Hebrews 6:16, does the word take on the meaning of end or conclusion: the oath ends the dispute. The Christian context remains that of a concrete or practical reality: the limits of the world, or the conclusion of a matter.
G4009.portee: This word reminds the reader that the Gospel is not reserved for a close or local elite: it extends to the ends of the earth, even to the most distant peoples. The queen of the South, coming from very far away, becomes a figure of those who seek divine wisdom, no matter where they live. It also speaks of the conclusive power of the word: it does not float indefinitely, it reaches its goals and produces decisive results.

sens: Ancient city of Mysia, in Asia Minor (present-day Turkey)
One of the seven Churches of Asia to which Revelation addresses a message
G4010.detail:
1. Pergamum is a large port city in the ancient region of Mysia, located on the western coast of Asia Minor (present-day Turkey). It was an important center of culture, commerce, and political power, famous for its library and temples. John first mentions it when he lists the seven Churches receiving his book (Revelation 1:11).

2. Pergamum appears as one of the seven Churches that the risen Lord addresses in Revelation. The message to the Church in Pergamum (Revelation 2:12) highlights its particular situation: it remains "where the throne of Satan is" — likely due to the prominence of pagan worship and the political power that reigns there — and it must remain faithful despite the pressures and seductions of the surrounding world.
G4010.origine: Pergamum is a real historical city of ancient Greek Asia Minor, whose Greek name Πέργαμος (Pergamos) is well attested by ancient authors such as Xenophon and Pausanias. The name may derive from the Greek word "perg-" meaning fortification or citadel, which would correspond to its nature as a fortified city. The Bible uses the Greek name as it was known at the time of the New Testament.
G4010.emploi: Pergamum appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in Revelation. John cites it among the seven Churches of Asia when he receives the order to send his book of visions (Revelation 1:11), then he addresses a specific message to the Church established in this city (Revelation 2:12). This selection of the seven Churches is not random: they likely represent the major Christian communities of the Roman province of Asia towards the end of the first century. Pergamum, as a major political and religious center, occupies a significant place in this circuit of seven messages.
G4010.portee: For the Christian reader, Pergamum reminds us that the Church of Jesus does not exist outside the world, but must maintain its faith despite the cultural and religious pressures that surround it. The message to Pergamum invites faithfulness to the name of Christ even when living in the heart of a city hostile to faith, showing that victory lies not in flight but in courageous perseverance.

sens: City in the region of Pamphylia, in Asia Minor (present-day Turkey)
G4011.detail: 1. Perga is a port city in Pamphylia, a coastal region of Asia Minor. Paul and Barnabas arrive there after their crossing from Cyprus at the beginning of the first missionary journey (Acts 13:13). It is here that John Mark leaves them to return to Jerusalem, which will later cause tension between Paul and Barnabas. On the return trip, Paul and Barnabas pass through again and preach the word before descending to the port of Attalia (Acts 14:25).
G4011.origine: The Greek name Pergē designates this important city of Pamphylia, known in antiquity for its maritime trade and prosperous urban life. Its spelling and geographical location are well attested in ancient historical and geographical sources.
G4011.emploi: Perga appears three times in the New Testament, all in the Acts of the Apostles. It is mentioned in the account of Paul’s first missionary journey (chapters 13-14): Paul arrives there in 13:13, departs in 13:14, and then passes through again in 14:25. These mentions show that the city was an important stop on the route of evangelization, first on the way out, then on the return.

sens: around, surrounding (spatial sense)
about, regarding (what is being discussed)
approximately, about (for time)
in favor of, for (what one defends or requests)
on behalf of, from (what is reported)
beyond, out of (in compounds)
G4012.detail:
1. In ancient Greek, this word primarily denotes the space around something: John's clothing is made of camel's hair (Matthew 3:4 — around his body). This is the initial image, spatial.
2. However, the Bible mainly uses it for what is being discussed, what is debated or reported: Herod asks his scholars to report information about the child (Matthew 2:8), and John's disciples have a dispute concerning purification (John 3:25). This is the primary meaning.
3. For time, it expresses an approximate duration: noon (Matthew 20:3, 5, 6, 9), dawn (Acts 10:3), or "at what hour" Jesus died (Matthew 27:46).
4. It can also indicate the purpose for which one acts or prays: Paul says "we continually pray for you" (2 Thessalonians 1:11), and Jesus asks that the cup be taken away "for" (that is, because of) our sins.
5. It can report what is said or heard: one bears witness to the things accomplished by Jesus (John 21:24).
6. In composition (at the beginning of other words), it expresses the idea of encirclement (περιβάλλω: to clothe) or surplus (περισσεύω: to abound).
G4012.origine: This word comes from an Indo-European root meaning "to turn around." In classical Greek, it initially has a spatial sense: around, all around. The corresponding Hebrew word is often עַל ("on," "concerning"), and Aramaic uses פּום ("mouth," by extension "what is said about"). The preposition has shifted from the spatial to the causal and discursive: one speaks of what surrounds a question, what concerns it.
G4012.emploi: This preposition is extremely common in the New Testament (306 occurrences). It is constructed with the genitive ("concerning someone") or the accusative ("around something"). In the Gospels, it serves to pose questions and debates: about the day and hour (Mark 13:32), about purification (John 3:25), about traditions (Luke 12:26). It often expresses the subject of a conversation or preaching (Luke 1:1: "the events that have been fulfilled among us"). In Acts and the Epistles, it becomes the tool of testimony and doctrine: one speaks "of" the resurrection (Acts 2), one prays "for" the brothers, one addresses the "things" that pertain to faith (2 Timothy 6:4). The meaning often oscillates between "about" and "for the sake of" depending on the context.
G4012.portee: This preposition is the word of transmission and sharing. It connects the speaker to the listener through a common reality: what is being discussed. For the biblical reader, it is the word that signals where attention is directed: on the little king that the magi seek, on the purification that divides, on the resurrection that defines faith. Understanding that the Bible speaks "concerning" Jesus (John 5:39) or "concerning" our brothers (Ephesians 6:22) invites recognition of these statements as testimonies addressed to faith, not abstractions.

sens: To lead someone by guiding them from one place to another
To go from one place to another by traversing an area
To travel without a specific direction, to feel one's way
G4013.detail:
1. To lead or bring someone along: this is the idea of making someone walk along a route (1 Corinthians 9:5 speaks of a woman who is "led" along with one).
2. To go from place to place in an area, regularly traversing it to accomplish a mission: Jesus "traveled through" all of Galilee teaching and healing (Matthew 4:23), or the villages to teach (Mark 6:6). This is a repeated and methodical movement within a territory.
3. To move without a clear direction, feeling one's way: the blind man struck by blindness in Acts 13:11 "feels his way" to find someone to guide him. The movement here is hesitant and uncertain.
G4013.origine: The word is composed of "peri" (around) and "ago" (to lead, to bring). The basic idea is therefore "to lead around." In Hebrew, the Septuagint (Greek translation) often renders this word with verbs meaning to walk, to turn, or to pass (halak, sâbab, âbar), all of which express the idea of moving in space, particularly around a place or region.
G4013.emploi: The verb appears 6 times in the New Testament. In Matthew, it regularly describes Jesus' itinerant activity: he "travels through" Galilee (4:23) and "travels through" the cities and villages (9:35), meaning he moves systematically to teach and heal. Mark uses it similarly (6:6). In Matthew 23:15, it also indicates intensive movement: the Pharisees "travel" land and sea (meaning an active and laborious crossing) to make a proselyte. In Acts 13:11, the verb takes on a different shade with the idea of feeling one's way, moving blindly. In 1 Corinthians 9:5, it simply means "to bring along." The meaning remains linked to movement but varies according to context: organized missionary activity, or simple accompanied movement.
G4013.portee: This word speaks to readers about active engagement: Jesus does not remain passive; he actively "travels through" regions to teach and heal. This illustrates his concrete dedication to the crowds. Likewise, for today's believer, the verb invites reflection on the Christian walk: a living faith is not stationary; it moves, it acts, it carries its message. When one "travels through" for God, it is with intention and commitment.

sens: To physically take away what surrounds or covers something
To drop or detach (in nautical language)
To withdraw, to make disappear (in a figurative sense)
G4014.detail:
1. The word evokes the action of removing an object that covers or surrounds something: a garment (the tunic), a ring (Genesis 41:42), a veil. In 2 Corinthians 3:16, when the heart turns to the Lord, the veil is removed — the obstacle that hid the clarity of God disappears.
2. In maritime travel accounts, the word denotes the action of dropping or detaching: dropping the anchors of the ship (Acts 27:40). The nautical sense continues in Acts 28:13 where "following the coast" literally means navigating along the shore, the ship moving away from what surrounds it.
3. In a figurative sense, the verb means to completely remove, to make disappear: to take away sins (Hebrews 10:11) or to withdraw hope (Acts 27:20, where "losing hope" expresses that all hope has been taken away by the violence of the storm).
G4014.origine: The word is composed of peri- ("around") and aireo ("to remove, to take"). The basic image is that of removing what surrounds: hence "to remove," "to take away." The prefix peri- reinforces the idea of complete detachment. In the Greek translations of the Old Testament, this verb often translates the Hebrew sure in the causative form ("to divert, to turn away"), which also expresses this idea of removal or diversion.
G4014.emploi: The verb appears 5 times in the New Testament, mainly in Acts and once in 2 Corinthians. In Acts 27:40, the sailors drop the anchors of the ship during the storm. In Acts 28:13, the context is nautical: the ship follows the coast. In 2 Corinthians 3:16, it refers to the veil removed from the heart at conversion. In Acts 27:20, hope is taken away from the shipwrecked. In Hebrews 10:11, it is the removal of sins that the sacrifice cannot accomplish. The meaning oscillates between the concrete (removing an object, detaching) and the figurative (making an obstacle or burden disappear).
G4014.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that conversion removes the obstacle that separates us from God: the veil falls (2 Corinthians 3:16). It also evokes that only the perfect sacrifice of Christ truly removes sins (Hebrews 10:11), which the repeated sacrifices of the Law could not do. For those traversing the storms of life, it is a word of hope: even when hope seems removed, God remains in control.

sens: To shine, emit a bright light around something or someone
To illuminate everything surrounding, enveloping in light
G4015.detail:
1. The verb describes a light that shines intensely by radiating around a central point. It is a dazzling light that is not static but spreads, enveloping. When Paul is on his way to Damascus, "a light from heaven shone around him" (Acts 9:3): this is not just a simple glow, but a sudden and powerful radiance that illuminates him from all sides.
2. The word can also emphasize the enveloping and dominating effect of this light. It does not shine from one side; it completely surrounds. In Acts 22:6, Paul specifies that "a great light from heaven shone around me": this is a total, luminous experience that fills the space around him.
G4015.origine: The word is composed of "peri" (around) and "astraptō" (to shine, emit a flash). The root "astraptō" evokes the lightning that illuminates the sky — an image of violence and luminous power. By combining them, "periastraptō" adds the idea of radiation all around: the light is not directed; it diffuses.
G4015.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the account of Paul's conversion. In Acts 9:3 and 22:6, it describes the same scene: the heavenly light that strikes Paul on the road to Damascus. In both cases, it is a light "coming from heaven," extraordinary and sudden. The choice of this verb emphasizes the dazzling and enveloping nature of this theophany — a total visual experience that marks a definitive turning point.
G4015.portee: This word helps the reader understand the intensity and physical reality of Paul's experience. It is not an inner or symbolic vision; it is a physical, visible light that strikes him from all sides. For the believer, it serves as a reminder that God can reveal Himself in a dazzling and undeniable way, overwhelming those who encounter Him.

sens: To wrap something around someone, to cover them with a garment
To put on clothing, to dress oneself
To wear clothes, to be dressed in a particular manner
To completely cover (in a figurative sense)
G4016.detail:
1. The primary, very concrete meaning is to throw a garment around a person to cover them. It is the image of the physical gesture: one takes a coat, a dress, and wraps it around someone. John 19:2 provides a poignant example: the soldiers dressed Jesus in a purple robe as mockery.
2. By natural extension, the word means to put on clothing, to dress oneself. Acts 12:8 simply shows this: Peter girds himself and puts on his shoes. The middle voice (to clothe oneself) appears in passages where someone is said to have clothed themselves in such garments.
3. The word is also used to describe the state of someone wearing a certain garment, who is dressed in a certain way. A young man "dressed in a white robe" (Mark 16:5): this is a description of his appearance. The twenty-four elders seated around the throne are "clothed in white garments" (Revelation 4:4).
4. Finally, it can mean to cover or envelop in a broader and figurative sense: an angel "wrapped in a cloud" (Revelation 10:1). Here, the cloud completely surrounds him, covering him like a garment.
G4016.origine: The Greek word comes from *peri* (around) and *ballō* (to throw, to cast). The basic image is thus to throw something around, to envelop by projecting. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it mainly translates *kāsāh* (to cover) and *lābash* (to clothe), which have the same idea: to cover something or someone. The family of the word also includes *emballō* (to throw in) and *epibollē* (a glance, a throw of sight).
G4016.emploi: The word appears 23 times in the New Testament, mainly in Revelation and the Gospels. It is used both in the passive (to be clothed, to be dressed) and in the middle (to clothe oneself). In the Gospels, it describes how people are clothed: Jesus naked clothed (Matthew 25:36, 38, 43), Jesus dressed in purple by the soldiers (John 19:2), the young man at the resurrection in his white robe (Mark 16:5). In Revelation, the word becomes particularly frequent to describe the garments of celestial beings and characters from God's realm: the elders in white garments, the woman clothed with the sun, the angels wrapped or adorned with various adornments. The context is often one of glory, power, or identification with God.
G4016.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of the body and appearance in Christian life. Jesus teaches in Matthew 6:29 that the lilies of the field are dressed better than Solomon: God takes care of His creatures. The command to clothe the naked (Matthew 25:36) becomes a concrete act of charity, a sign of Christ's love. In Revelation, white or glorious garments symbolize purity and honor before God. Finally, the nakedness that must be covered represents all forms of distress and need: to clothe is to restore human dignity.

sens: To cast one's eyes around oneself, to examine what surrounds
To look for someone or something among others
To observe attentively the present people
To inspect a place by scanning it visually
G4017.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of turning and moving one's gaze in different directions: the eyes sweep the space to see what is there. It is a natural gesture one makes when wanting to have an overview (Mark 9:8: "the disciples looked all around").
2. It also involves searching for someone partially hidden or lost in the crowd (Mark 5:32: Jesus "looked around to see who had done this"), as if scanning the audience to locate a person.
3. The word can express an observation that judges and evaluates those being looked at, with a particular intention or emotion: anger, affection, teaching (Mark 3:5: Jesus "looked around at them with anger").
4. It is also used to describe the careful inspection of a place as a whole (Mark 11:11: Jesus "considered everything" when visiting the temple), a complete visual examination before leaving or acting.
G4017.origine: The word is composed of peri ("around") and blépō ("to look"). The basic image is that of a gaze that turns around oneself, embracing the space circularly. This composition suggests an examination or observation that is not fixed but explores. The verb appears mainly in Mark, the evangelist who loves to describe the gestures and attitudes of Jesus.
G4017.emploi: The verb appears 7 times in the New Testament, concentrated in the Gospel of Mark (6 occurrences) and once in Luke. Mark uses it to show Jesus observing His disciples or the crowd during decisive moments: healing a man (3:5), recognizing His true family (3:34), detecting who touched Him (5:32), teaching about wealth (10:23), arriving at the temple (11:11). The verb also appears at the moment of the Transfiguration (9:8). It is a verb of eye movement that enriches the narrative by showing the character's intention (to seek, to evaluate, to examine).
G4017.portee: This verb reminds us that Jesus' gaze was never passive or distracted. He truly saw the people and situations around Him, sometimes with compassion, sometimes with indignation at evil. For the reader, this invites a benevolent vigilance: to be present to others, to truly see them, and not to remain indifferent to what is happening around oneself.

sens: that which envelops the body, fabric or cloth worn on oneself
coat, cape, or loose garment
veil or covering for the face and hair
figuratively: that which envelops, that which covers
G4018.detail:
1. The word literally refers to a garment or a coat, something thrown around the body to cover and protect it. In Hebrews 1:12, the heavens and the earth are compared to a garment that God "will roll up like a cloak": the image suggests something flexible and perishable, that can be folded, changed, or removed (Hebrews 1:12).
2. In a more specific sense, the word can refer to a veil or hair covering the head and shoulders. In 1 Corinthians 11:15, Paul states that a woman's "hair" has been given to her as a natural veil, that is, as an adornment and covering appropriate to her nature (1 Corinthians 11:15).
3. Beyond the physical sense, the word can metaphorically express anything that envelops or covers, such as a spiritual cloak or protective covering.
G4018.origine: The word comes from περιβάλλω (periballô), "to throw around, to envelop," composed of περί (péri), "around," and βάλλω (ballô), "to throw." It thus designates what is "thrown around" the body. This family of words corresponds in Hebrew to terms like כְּסוּת (kesut) and לְבוּשׁ (lebûsh), which express clothing, coat, and covering.
G4018.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Hebrews 1:12, it is a quotation from the Old Testament where the image of the garment symbolizes the transient and changeable nature of creation: the heavens will disappear like a worn-out cloak. In 1 Corinthians 11:15, the context is that of modesty and propriety in worship: Paul speaks of a woman's hair as a natural covering given to her by God, emphasizing the created order and the proprieties of Christian worship.
G4018.portee: This word reminds us that every garment, every covering is a gift from God — it provides dignity and protection. For the Corinthians, this image invites respect for the natural order and the honor of the body, both for women and men. More broadly, the image of the garment in Hebrews humbles us: if even the visible universe is but a robe that God can change, true stability is found only in Him.

sens: To bind around something, as with a band or cloth
To completely surround a part of the body
To immobilize by wrapping
G4019.detail:
1. The word describes the action of binding or tying something around an object. In John 11:44, it refers to the strips that wrap around the feet and hands of the resurrected Lazarus: "his feet and hands bound with strips of linen."
2. The meaning extends to the idea of completely surrounding, covering. The face of the dead is "wrapped in a cloth": the fabric wraps and conceals the face.
3. The action produces an effect of immobilization or restraint: the strips tightly bind and hold, preparing the body for burial according to Jewish customs.
G4019.origine: The Greek word is composed of "peri" (around) and "deô" (to bind, to tie). It literally depicts the action of binding around. This image of wrapping applies both to the concrete domain (clothing, strips) and to the figurative domain (that which surrounds, embraces, or imprisons).
G4019.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in John 11:44, during the resurrection of Lazarus. The context is that of Jewish burial: the body is wrapped in cloths and strips. Jesus then commands that he be unbound from these ties so that he may come out alive from the tomb. This concrete detail underscores both the authenticity of death and the power of resurrection.
G4019.portee: This mention of the strips reminds us that Jesus resurrects not a ghost, but a real body that was truly dead and buried. It also shows that resurrection brings freedom: Lazarus must be unbound to walk, foreshadowing the freedom that Christ gives through His own resurrection.

sens: To waste one's effort on unimportant things
To show idle and malicious curiosity about the affairs of others
To interfere in the affairs of others without being invited
G4020.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to waste one's work and energy on vain and insignificant things — activities without lasting fruit or value. It is the image of a hand that flails without profit, exhausting itself for nothing (2 Thessalonians 3:11).
2. More specifically, it is to show unhealthy curiosity, to turn one's attention to gossip, rumors, the secrets of others — this desire to know and report that characterizes the busybody. The Thessalonians mentioned by Paul are idlers who, instead of working, spend their energy scrutinizing the lives of others.
3. In summary: it is to meddle in affairs that do not concern you, to intervene where you have not been invited, to engage in what is called "busybodying" — being the one whom everyone says cannot leave others in peace.
G4020.origine: The word is composed of "peri" (around, on all sides) and "ergazomai" (to work, to be busy). The image is that of circular agitation, of activity that goes in circles: one stirs, one fusses, one digs here and there, but without direction or true purpose. It is work that "goes around" things instead of attaching itself usefully to them.
G4020.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament: in 2 Thessalonians 3:11, where Paul reproaches certain members of the church for not working with their hands but for "meddling in trivialities." Paul contrasts harmful idleness (doing nothing for oneself) with meddling in the affairs of others: those who refuse honest work fill their time by snooping, gossiping, and quarreling about others. It is a characteristic trait of those who disturb the peace of the community.
G4020.portee: This word invites the reader to examine their use of time and motivations: do we work diligently to provide for ourselves and others, or do we waste our energy on idle curiosities and gossip? Paul reminds us that the service of Christ is measured by concrete works and a worthy life, not by superficial agitation. It is a call to true freedom: the kind that arises from useful work and respect for boundaries, not from the dependence created by the life of parasites and busybodies.

sens: One who meddles in everything, who sticks their nose everywhere
One who practices mysterious or magical arts
One who exceeds ordinary measure, who is excessive
G4021.detail:
1. A curious person is one who cannot help but interfere in the affairs of others, ask indiscreet questions, and report what they have heard. This is a form of intrusive and gossiping chatter. In 1 Timothy 5:13, the Apostle Paul describes widows who, instead of keeping themselves honorably occupied, go from house to house, being gossips and busybodies, meaning they pry into the affairs of others and spread rumors.
2. A curious thing can also refer to what is mysterious, occult, belonging to the realm of the hidden and supernatural — particularly magical practices. In Acts 19:19, the converts from Ephesus burn their books of curious arts (or rather magical arts), acknowledging that these practices belong to a spiritual realm contrary to faith in Christ.
3. The word can finally qualify what is excessive, over-elaborate, going beyond what is necessary — a kind of excess or superfluous refinement.
G4021.origine: The Greek word περίεργος is composed of περί (around, beyond) and ἔργον (work, labor). The basic image is that of something that 'works around' or 'exceeds the measure of normal work.' This composition explains why the word can mean both 'meddling in what does not concern one' (going beyond one's role) and 'pertaining to the occult or mysterious realm' (what is out of the ordinary). The Latin translation 'curiosus' has given its meaning to the French 'curieux,' although our word 'curiosity' has also taken on a positive meaning that the ancient Greek does not have here.
G4021.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In 1 Timothy 5:13, Paul reproaches the younger widows for being 'busybodies,' meaning they occupy themselves with what does not concern them, due to their idleness. In Acts 19:19, it describes the 'magical arts' or 'curious arts' that the Ephesians burn after their conversion. These two usages show that the word describes what exceeds proper limits: either by intruding indiscreetly into the affairs of others or by being drawn to suspicious and occult spiritual practices.
G4021.portee: This word invites the Christian to examine their thoughts and words: do they always seek to know what does not concern them? Do they listen to or spread gossip? It also reminds us that unhealthy curiosity about the mysterious and the occult — what seeks to give power without going through God — is a spiritual trap. The solution, as for the Ephesians, is to resolutely turn one's heart toward Christ and away from these dangerous fascinations.

sens: To move from one place to another, wandering back and forth
(of a person) to go from house to house to carry out a trade or activity
To travel or move without a fixed dwelling
G4022.detail:
1. The literal meaning is that of a person who moves around, going from one place to another without staying in the same location. In Hebrews 11:37, persecuted prophets 'went here and there, dressed in sheep skins and goat skins': they wander, chased from everywhere, having no stable home.
2. More often, the word refers to the act of going from house to house or places to carry out a trade or task. In Acts 19:13, the Jewish exorcists 'went' from house to house to cast out demons by invoking the name of Jesus. This is a regular, methodical movement from one dwelling to another.
3. In 1 Timothy 5:13, idle women 'went' from house to house: here, the idea is one of social wandering, a continuous circulation that leads them to gossip and do harm. Physical movement becomes a sign of moral restlessness.
G4022.origine: The word is composed of the prefix 'peri' (around) and the verb 'erchomai' (to go, to come). The image is that of a walk that turns around, traversing a space in all directions. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, a similar idea is found with the verb 'sâbab' (to turn around, to encircle), which the Greek version uses to translate passages where one walks in circulation.
G4022.emploi: This verb appears three times in the New Testament, always to describe a type of habitual or itinerant movement. In Acts 19:13, it describes the Jewish exorcists who go from house to house to carry out their trade. In 1 Timothy 5:13, it depicts young widows who become idle and socially wander. In Hebrews 11:37, it evokes the fate of the faithful ancient prophets, wandering without stable refuge. In all cases, the word emphasizes continuous movement, without a fixed anchor point.
G4022.portee: This verb invites us to meditate on two opposing realities. On one hand, going here and there can be a service: the exorcists moved to cast out demons (although without true authority). On the other hand, wandering without a dwelling has been the lot of faithful prophets, a sign of their persecution but also of their trust in God. The word also speaks to the danger of idleness: when one has no stable objective, one risks becoming a gossip and harmful, like those widows who began to gossip from house to house.

sens: to surround, to circumscribe
to seize, to invade
to contain, to include (in the sense of to comprise)
G4023.detail:
1. The primary meaning is spatial and concrete: to surround something to hold it, to circumscribe or delimit it. It conveys the idea of closing around.

2. When this verb speaks of an emotion or sensation, it means that it completely overwhelms you, as if it surrounds you. In Luke 5:9, fear 'seized' Simon Peter and his companions: it enveloped them on all sides at the moment they witnessed the miracle of the catch of fish.

3. In a broader and abstract sense, 'to contain' means to enclose or comprise something. When it is said that a Scripture 'says' (or comprises) something, it means it states it, it includes it within itself. In 1 Peter 2:6, the Scripture contains the promise regarding the cornerstone.
G4023.origine: The word comes from the prefix 'peri' (around) and the verb 'echô' (to hold, to have). The basic image is 'to hold around': to surround to seize, or to seize by surrounding. This figurative composition (circular action producing an effect) is very Greek. The verb translates Hebrew words meaning to circumscribe or to retain.
G4023.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament. In Luke 5:9, it describes the emotion that seizes the disciples in the face of the miracle: a fear that completely envelops them. In 1 Peter 2:6, it functions in a more abstract and grammatical way to say that a scriptural word 'contains' or 'states' a promise. The usage thus shifts from the concrete sense (being seized by an emotion) to the abstract sense (to comprise, to include a thought or word).
G4023.portee: This word reminds us that we are never neutral before God and His work: true miracles 'seize' us, they overwhelm us with respect and fear. The presence of God is not information that one hears from afar; it takes hold of us, it surrounds us. This invites us not to remain indifferent in the face of the sacred.

sens: To put a belt or band around the waist
To gird oneself: to prepare for action or service
To hold firmly, to remain stable in truth and justice
G4024.detail:
1. To gird literally means to wrap a belt around one's waist or loins. It is a concrete gesture that prepares the body for action — one girds a loose garment so that it does not hinder during work or running. In Revelation 1:13 and 15:6, the Son of Man and the angels wear golden girdles, symbolizing glory and heavenly dignity.
2. To gird oneself (reflexive form) means to take the attitude of a servant who is ready to serve. In Luke 12:37, the happy master will gird himself to serve his faithful servants — an act of humility and absolute devotion. In Luke 17:8, the servant is told to gird himself before serving the meal.
3. Figuratively (Ephesians 6:14), "girding one's loins with truth" means to hold firmly to the truth as spiritual armor, to remain stable and resolute in faith in the face of evil attacks. It is less an action than a posture of vigilance and solidity.
G4024.origine: The Greek word is composed of "peri" (around) and "zônnumi" (to gird, to bind around). It primarily translates the Hebrew verbs "hagar" and "azar" which have the same meaning of girding or surrounding. The image is that of wrapping something around the body or waist.
G4024.emploi: The verb appears 6 times in the New Testament, mostly in Luke. In Luke 12:35, 37 and 17:8, it describes practical gestures of servitude: girding one's loins to be ready for service, or girding oneself to serve at the table. It is the attitude of the diligent and humble servant. In Revelation 1:13 and 15:6, it refers to heavenly and glorious garments. In Ephesians 6:14, Paul uses the verb figuratively: girding one's loins with truth becomes a spiritual and moral preparation to resist the schemes of the devil.
G4024.portee: This word teaches Christians two essential things. First, it shows that authentic service, even that of the Lord Himself, involves humility and practical devotion — to gird oneself is to make oneself available and active for others. Secondly, it reminds that spiritual life requires preparation: to gird oneself with truth is to anchor one's life in the Word of God to stand firm in the battles of faith.

sens: The act of putting adornment around oneself
An object worn as decoration on the body
That which beautifies the outward appearance
G4025.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the act of putting adornment or an accessory around oneself: it is the gesture of adorning oneself. One thinks of the daily acts of dressing and beautifying (1 Peter 3:3).
2. By extension, it refers to the ornament itself, the adornment: jewelry, precious clothing, anything worn to shine or attract. In 1 Peter 3:3, Peter lists these ornaments (braided hair, gold) that women wore.
3. More broadly, it encompasses anything that beautifies the outward appearance, anything that seeks to please through splendor. Peter contrasts it with the inner adornment of the heart.
G4025.origine: The word comes from the root "perithesis" formed from "peri" (around) and "thesis" (the act of placing). It literally describes the act of putting something around oneself. The related verb, "perititheêmi", means to place around, to clothe oneself.
G4025.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 3:3. Peter uses it in an exhortation to Christian women regarding their attire: he warns them against excessive confidence in outward adornment (braided hair, gold jewelry, precious clothing). Its use is therefore moral and pastoral: it critiques the pride of appearance to promote inner beauty, hidden within the heart.
G4025.portee: This word reminds Christians that true beauty does not come from what shines on the outside. Peter invites to distinguish what is superficial and fleeting from what has true value: the hidden and lasting character of the heart. It is a relevant word about the relationship to consumption, appearances, and identity.

sens: To place someone or something around a place
To stand around someone
To avoid, to flee (figurative sense)
G4026.detail:
1. The primary meaning of the word is physical: to arrange people or things in a circle around a center. The crowd "surrounds" Jesus in Bethany (John 11:42): it encircles Him, it is all around Him.
2. This same concrete meaning becomes a living picture: the crowd "surrounds" Jesus, the Jews "surround" Paul in court (Acts 25:7). The image is that of people placed in a circle, close and attentive.
3. In a figurative sense, particularly in Paul's letters, the word means "to avoid" or "to turn away from." When Paul commands to turn away from "profane" discussions (2 Timothy 2:16) and "foolish controversies" (Titus 3:9), he uses this verb to say: turn away from these things, do not approach them, as one turns away from an obstacle.
G4026.origine: The word is composed of "peri" (around) and "histêmi" (to stand, to place). The basic image is that of standing around something. In Hebrew, the verbs סָבַב (sabab, to surround) and נָצַב (nitsav, to stand) express similar concepts. The transition to the figurative sense — to avoid, to turn away — is natural: to turn away becomes the opposite of approaching.
G4026.emploi: The verb appears four times in the New Testament. In John 11:42 and Acts 25:7, it literally describes people standing around someone. In 2 Timothy 2:16 and Titus 3:9, the meaning shifts: it is no longer about physically placing oneself around a person, but about morally turning away from something — futile discussions, sterile quarrels. Paul uses the verb in the middle or passive reflexive voice to express an active rejection: the Christian must distance themselves, turn away from what would lead them to ungodliness.
G4026.portee: This word reminds us that our position regarding teachings and words matters. Just as one can physically surround oneself with people, one can morally attract thoughts or sterile disputes. Paul urges Christians to do the opposite: to consciously avoid what does not edify and distracts from piety. It is a call to vigilance and separation from the vain.

sens: Waste, rubbish, what is swept away
Despised person, outcast of society
G4027.detail: 1. A sweepings is literally waste, rubbish, what is gathered when cleaning the floor — the image is that of worthless dirt that is thrown away. 2. Paul uses it figuratively to describe his condition: he and his companions are treated as the refuse, the waste of society, those who are despised and rejected (1 Corinthians 4:13). It is the ultimate insult, as they are equated with what is most vile and useless.
G4027.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "to purify completely" (peri = around, all sides; cathairô = to purify). A sweepings is therefore what is rejected during a thorough cleaning — the rubbish removed to ensure everything is pure. The underlying Hebrew word in the Septuagint (the Greek Bible of the Old Testament) generally meant "ransom" or "expiation," which shows how the meaning could designate both the sacrifice offered for purification and the waste that is removed.
G4027.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament: in 1 Corinthians 4:13, where Paul speaks of himself and his fellow apostles. They are slandered, persecuted, treated with contempt by those around them, and Paul uses this extreme image — that of a sweepings, of waste — to show the intensity of the disdain they endure. It is a striking contrast: they who bring the Gospel are rejected as the worst of refuse.
G4027.portee: This passage invites us to recognize that faithful service to God can attract the world's disdain and humiliation. But by using such a crude word, Paul also shows that those who follow Christ must be ready to accept dishonor without retaliating with slander. It is a lesson in humility and patience in persecution.

sens: To completely cover, hide
To wrap in a material for protection or decoration
To deliberately mask to harm or humiliate
G4028.detail:
1. The word denotes the action of completely covering something: to cover, to wrap on all sides. It is an act that hides what is underneath or transforms its appearance. In Hebrews 9:4, the ark of the covenant is "entirely covered with gold": the gold completely envelops it, protects it, and magnifies it.
2. When this covering is applied intentionally, it is often to protect something precious or to make it conform to its sacred use. The gold that covers the ark expresses its divine and untouchable character.
3. The word takes on a nuance of violence and humiliation when it comes to veiling a human face. In Mark 14:65 and Luke 22:64, Jesus has his face veiled — hidden, masked — while he is struck or tortured, which exacerbates his humiliation: he is prevented from seeing and rendered defenseless.
G4028.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "peri-" (around, everywhere) and the verb "kalúptō" (to cover). This composition expresses a complete covering, encompassing from all sides. In ancient Hebrew, the verbs translated by this word (such as "kasah" to cover, or "shabats" to coat) carry the same idea: to put a cover, an envelope.
G4028.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Greek New Testament. Twice, it describes the veiling of Jesus' face during his Passion (Mark 14:65; Luke 22:64): this gesture is an act of mockery and mistreatment, making any resistance or dignity impossible. Once, it speaks of the gold covering of the ark of the covenant (Hebrews 9:4): here, the covering is sacred, it protects and consecrates.
G4028.portee: The veiling of Jesus' face reveals how total his humiliation was: not only struck, but made blind and mute, deprived of his power to see and act. This poignant detail shows that Jesus endured an absolute dispossession for us. In contrast, the ark covered in gold reminds us that what is precious and divine in heaven is veiled from our earthly eyes, worthy of the greatest respect.

sens: To be placed around something or someone, to encircle
To wear, to be clothed in
To be surrounded, enveloped as by an atmosphere or presence
G4029.detail:
1. The primary meaning is literal: a millstone placed around the neck (Mark 9:42, Luke 17:2), an object placed around the body to weigh it down or mark it. The verb describes something that is wrapped or fixed around someone, like a chain worn (Acts 28:20: "this chain").
2. In the sense of "to wear" or "to have around oneself," the word denotes what belongs to someone personally, what characterizes them: weakness is the "lot" of every man, that is, what naturally surrounds him, what he is clothed in (Hebrews 5:2).
3. In a figurative sense, it is to be surrounded by an invisible but real presence: a "cloud of witnesses" surrounds us (Hebrews 12:1), not physically but as a moral atmosphere that encourages us to persevere in faith.
G4029.origine: The verb comes from the preposition "peri" (around) and the verb "keimaï" (to lie down, to be placed). The basic image is that of something placed, spread, or wrapped all around. It is a word that emphasizes immediate proximity, encirclement.
G4029.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, mainly in Luke and the Epistles. Mark and Luke use it for the shocking image of the millstone thrown around a man's neck: this is the most concrete and brutal sense. Paul uses it in Acts 28:20 to speak of his chain as a tangible reality he constantly bears. The Epistle to the Hebrews uses it in a figurative sense: the weakness we share (5:2) and especially this cloud of witnesses (12:1) that envelops us as a presence supporting our walk. The verb thus glides from the concrete (what is put around the body) to the spiritual (what surrounds us invisibly).
G4029.portee: This verb invites the reader to see spiritual realities as present and tangible as chains or millstones. The cloud of witnesses in Hebrews 12:1 reminds us that our race of faith is not solitary: we are surrounded by an invisible crowd of believers who watch us and encourage us. This gives flesh and presence to the invisible that supports us.

sens: Metallic headgear that protects the head in battle
Spiritual protection given by hope or salvation
G4030.detail:
1. A helmet is a piece of war equipment, a rigid headgear made of metal or leather that covers and defends the warrior's head against blows. It is a concrete and visible object, like the other weapons of the Roman soldier.
2. Paul uses this image of the helmet to speak of spiritual protection. In 1 Thessalonians 5:8, the "helmet" is the hope of salvation, which protects the Christian as armor protects a soldier. Similarly, in Ephesians 6:17, it refers to the helmet of salvation — the certainty of salvation in Christ, which defends the believer's soul against doubt and fear.
G4030.origine: The word comes from the Greek perikephalaïa, composed of peri ("around") and kephalé ("head"), literally meaning "that which surrounds the head." It is simply the descriptive name of this piece of war equipment. In the Greek Bible, it translates the Hebrew word qobáa, the helmet of the warrior or priest in the Old Testament.
G4030.emploi: The word helmet appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in Paul’s context of the spiritual armor of the Christian. In Ephesians 6:17, in the description of the believer's weapons, the helmet represents salvation — what we already possess in Christ and what protects us. In 1 Thessalonians 5:8, it symbolizes the hope of salvation, the confidence in the divine promise. Paul thus borrows from the everyday military image to show that faith needs this protection.
G4030.portee: For the believer, the helmet reminds us that salvation and hope are not luxuries, but vital protection. Just as a soldier puts on his armor before battle, the Christian must appropriate the assurance of his salvation in the face of trials and temptations. It is an invitation not to walk in fear or doubt, but in the certainty that Christ has already saved him.

sens: One who has complete control, dominion over something
One who exercises command or authority
One who possesses and directs a good or service
G4031.detail:
1. The word literally describes one who has a grip, who firmly holds something under control. In Acts 27:16, during the storm at sea, Paul and his companions "had difficulty mastering the lifeboat": it is the concrete image of taking hold, of effective domination over an object or situation.
2. By extension, "master" designates one who exercises authority, who commands and directs. It is a position of power and responsibility.
3. It can also evoke one who possesses something personally and is responsible for it, as a master possesses his goods or servants.
G4031.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "peri" (around) and "kratéô" (to hold, to dominate), a root that evokes the idea of strength and mastery. The primary image is that of power that envelops, that completely surrounds: one can only hold something if one has control over it from all sides. This root belongs to the family of Greek words expressing power and authority (such as "cratos," strength, or "krateô," to conquer).
G4031.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:16, during the account of Paul's shipwreck on the way to Rome. Paul and his companions struggle against the elements to "master" their lifeboat (the small boat attached to the ship): the context is one of physical struggle against waves and wind. The usage emphasizes the effort needed to maintain control of a situation or object in the face of opposing forces.
G4031.portee: This word reminds readers that true control of a situation does not come easily, especially in the face of the forces of nature or trials. It is a lesson in humility: even the apostle Paul can hardly tame the storm. But it also invites us to recognize that the one who maintains control, who "masters" the circumstances, demonstrates strength and wisdom in the face of adversity.

sens: To keep hidden, completely conceal
To withdraw from sight, to confine oneself
To keep secret, not reveal
G4032.detail: 1. The primary meaning is to hide something or someone completely and durably. Elizabeth hides for five months so as not to be seen (Luke 1:24): she withdraws from public life, remaining confined at home. 2. This verb evokes the idea of withdrawing from sight, voluntarily confining oneself. Elizabeth removes herself from the view of others during her pregnancy, reinforcing the image of an intentional and prolonged retreat. 3. The act of hiding often carries a dimension of reserve or secrecy: Elizabeth keeps to herself, at least in the eyes of others, what is happening to her, as if she wants to protect this extraordinary event.
G4032.origine: The word adds the prefix περί (around, all around) to the verb κρύπτω (to hide). This composition reinforces the idea of concealment: one hides not just partially, but completely from all sides. The root expresses the action of hiding or veiling, as if wrapping something to remove it from sight.
G4032.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 1:24. Elizabeth, after conceiving John the Baptist, hides for five months. This act of seclusion adds weight to the narrative: she had long awaited a child (Luke 1:7), and this miraculous pregnancy is so extraordinary that it preserves her from public judgment and prying eyes. Elizabeth's retreat expresses both humility (she does not proclaim her happiness) and protection (she sets herself apart to allow God to act quietly).
G4032.portee: Elizabeth's example of hiding shows that there is a time for silence and seclusion in the face of God's great works. This discretion is not shame or fear, but a form of respect for what the Lord is doing: she allows the miracle to develop away from the tumult of the world. For the believer, this suggests that not every action of God needs to be proclaimed immediately; there is wisdom in waiting for God's timing before sharing what He has accomplished.

sens: To encircle something on all sides
To besiege or capture
To enclose by blocking access
G4033.detail:
1. The word describes the action of completely surrounding something, forming a circle around it: like enemies approaching from all sides around a city. In Luke 19:43, Jesus announces that days will come when enemies will surround Jerusalem — they will encircle it with trenches to besiege it.
2. It refers more specifically to a military encirclement: troops that enclose a besieged city to suffocate it and force it to surrender. The image evokes a vise tightening.
3. The result is confinement: once surrounded, the city can no longer escape or receive help. Jesus speaks of an inevitable captivity approaching for Jerusalem.
G4033.origine: The word combines two Greek elements: the preposition « péri » (around) and the verb « kuklóô » (to form a circle, from which the French word « cycle » comes). This composition creates the idea of an action that turns around, encircling from all sides. The Hebrew verb it translates — « sabab » — also means « to turn around » and « to surround ». This root evokes circular movement, the round of enemies.
G4033.emploi: The verb « surround » appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 19:43, in this dramatic prophecy of Jesus about the destruction of Jerusalem. Jesus uses this term to describe the military siege that will come upon the city: its enemies will « surround » it with trenches. It is a precise military term, evoking the total blockade of a besieged city. The context is that of the prophecy of divine judgment on Jerusalem, which did not recognize Jesus as its Messiah.
G4033.portee: This word reminds Christians of the seriousness of Jesus' warnings and the inevitability of judgment for those who reject His grace. It also shows how Christ's love can express itself in the form of a warning: Jesus weeps over Jerusalem not out of anger, but because it exposes itself to destruction. For the reader, it is an invitation to welcome Jesus as Savior, rather than exposing oneself to the consequences of rejection.

sens: To shine, illuminate all around someone or something
To be suddenly surrounded by a bright light
To manifest one's presence or glory through radiant light
G4034.detail:
1. The concrete meaning is the action of shining intensely, radiating all around: a light suddenly and completely unfolds around a person or group. In Luke 2:9, it is the glory of the Lord that shines around the shepherds at night, creating a striking contrast between darkness and this divine radiance.

2. The word also describes the phenomenon of being surrounded by a brightness that surpasses anything ordinarily known. In Acts 26:13, Paul recounts how a light from heaven « shone around » him and his companions, specifying that its brightness surpassed that of the sun at midday: it is an illumination so intense that it exceeds natural light.

3. On a spiritual level, this verb expresses the manifestation of the divine presence or the glory of God through a visible and supernatural light. In both cases, it refers to moments when God becomes visible and reveals Himself in a striking manner to His servants.
G4034.origine: The Greek word is composed of the prefix « peri » (around) and « lampo » (to shine, to glow). This composition suggests a light that does not come from one side but radiates from all sides around the one who contemplates it. The word belongs to the family of verbs describing light and radiance, frequently used in the New Testament to speak of divine manifestations.
G4034.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, always in the context of theophany (divine appearances). In Luke 2:9, it describes the moment when the glory of the Lord envelops the shepherds during the announcement of Jesus' birth, causing them great fear. In Acts 26:13, Paul uses it to recount his encounter with the Lord on the road to Damascus: a supernatural light surrounds him, so bright that it surpasses the light of the sun. In both passages, the verb emphasizes the sudden, brilliant, and impressive nature of the divine manifestation.
G4034.portee: This verb reminds Christians that God's manifestations in history have often taken on a luminous and visible form, profoundly marking those who have received them. For both the shepherds and Paul, this light was accompanied by certainty and inner transformation: it was neither vague nor ordinary. By using this word, Scripture shows us that encountering God is an event that strikes, illuminates, and changes the one who witnesses it.

sens: To stay alive when others disappear
To survive an event
To be present at the time of a future event
G4035.detail:
1. The word describes one who remains alive while others die or disappear: it conveys the idea of surviving death. In 1 Thessalonians 4:15, Paul speaks of "we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord" — he refers to Christians who will still be alive at the coming of Jesus, in contrast to those who will have died.
2. More broadly, it means to remain, to exist after an event that could have swept you away. The word emphasizes the act of persisting, continuing to exist when other things have disappeared or changed.
3. In the context of the Church, Paul uses it to speak of those who will be present, alive, at the parousia: in 1 Thessalonians 4:17, the believers who are "left" will be "caught up together with them in the clouds." The emphasis is on the living presence at the decisive moment.
G4035.origine: The Greek word combines the prefix "peri" (around, near) and the root "leipo" (to leave, abandon). The idea is that of what remains, what is not taken away or rejected. The passive-reflexive form (deponent) reinforces the idea that the subject persists despite the circumstances. It is a word formed to express continuity and survival.
G4035.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in the same letter, 1 Thessalonians. Paul uses it solely to speak of Christians who will be alive at the return of Christ. It is a technical term in Pauline eschatological language — it does not simply refer to staying somewhere, but to persisting in life until this major event. The context of the two verses is identical: to reassure the Thessalonians that those who are alive will not be at a disadvantage compared to those who have already left this world.
G4035.portee: This word reminds the reader of a central truth of the Christian faith: the resurrection and the return of Christ. Paul uses this term to show that no one will be forgotten — neither the living nor the dead will be left behind. It is a word of hope and divine justice: all believers, dead or alive, will together participate in the final glory.

sens: Deeply saddened, overwhelmed by intense sorrow
Afflicted to the point that pain fills one's entire soul
Dejected by bad news or disappointment
G4036.detail:
1. The word describes a sorrow that goes beyond mere emotion: it is an affliction that grips the whole person. Jesus uses this expression in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:38, Mark 14:34) to describe the state of his soul in the face of the suffering that awaits him. It is a deep and overwhelming pain, that of a heart bearing the weight of an unbearable reality.
2. Sorrow can be provoked by bad news or disappointment. When the rich young man learns that he must sell all his possessions to follow Jesus, he "became very sad" (Luke 18:23) — a disappointment that overwhelms him because it calls into question his entire life.
3. Herod also feels this deep sorrow (Mark 6:26): the anxiety of seeing his oath compel him to commit an act whose painful consequences he senses fills him with an affliction that cannot be hidden.
G4036.origine: The word is composed of "peri" (around, entirely) and "lupos" (sorrow, pain). The image is that of a sorrow that envelops, completely surrounds the person, seizing them from all sides. This intensity is found in words of the same family: "lupeô" means "to grieve" or "to cause sorrow." In Hebrew, this feeling corresponds to the biblical expression of a soul seized by grief, as in the Psalms where one speaks of the soul that is deeply saddened.
G4036.emploi: The word appears only 5 times in the New Testament, always to express intense and sudden affliction. Three times, Jesus uses it for himself or it is in the context of his Passion that it is depicted. Mark 6:26 applies it to Herod facing the consequences of his oath. Luke 18:23-24 shows it in the rich young man confronted with the radical demand of the Gospel. In all cases, it is a sorrow that is not fleeting, but deeply marks the one who feels it. It always signals a confrontation with a reality that shakes.
G4036.portee: This word speaks to us of the reality of the suffering that Jesus himself experienced. By saying that his soul was "sorrowful unto death," he validates the depth of human pain and does not ask us to deny it. He also teaches us that following him radically can cost us dearly — as it did for the rich young man — and that this trial is real. But by going through this sorrow, Jesus opened a path of resurrection and life beyond pain.

sens: To stay in place in expectation, awaiting an event or a promise
To count on something that is to be realized
G4037.detail:
1. To wait means to stay in place, not leaving, while expecting something to happen. The disciples in Jerusalem must "wait" for the promise of the Father — that is, to remain there rather than disperse, counting on the coming of the Holy Spirit that Jesus has announced to them (Acts 1:4). It is an active, patient, and confident waiting.
2. It is also to place one's hope in something certain to come. The one who waits does not doubt that the thing will happen; they suspend their present action based on a guaranteed future reality. Biblical waiting is never passive or uncertain: it relies on a divine word or a reliable promise.
G4037.origine: The Greek verb perimenō is composed of the prefix peri ("around," "during") and the verb menō ("to stay," "to remain"). The basic image is that of staying in place, persevering. In Hebrew, Psalm 49:18 uses a word of the same family (qavah) which also means "to wait with confidence." This word always evokes a founded expectation, not a mere pause or indecision.
G4037.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 1:4, where Jesus commands the apostles to wait in Jerusalem before going on mission. It is in this context of the promise of the Father — the outpouring of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost — that the verb takes on its full weight. Waiting here is not inaction: it is an obedience that prepares the disciples to receive the power of God. The waiting is limited in time (ten days) and certain in its object.
G4037.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us of the importance of obeying God's orders rather than rushing ahead.
