3. The word can also express the idea of fleeing or taking off quickly away from danger: the woman of Revelation "flew" to the wilderness to escape the serpent's persecution, carried by the two wings of the great eagle (Revelation 12:14).
G4072.origine: The Greek word πέτομαι comes from a root that evokes the flapping of wings and light movement. In the Greek Old Testament, it generally translates the Hebrew verb עוּף (to fly), which designates the same movement of winged creatures. The verb belongs to a family of Greek words related to flight and soaring, and can take a more intensive form (πετάομαι) in some manuscripts.
G4072.emploi: The verb "to fly" appears five times in the New Testament, all in the Revelation of John. It is used to describe the movement of celestial creatures and angels: one of the four living creatures resembles an eagle that flies (Revelation 4:7), an eagle cries in the sky (Revelation 8:13), a woman flies to the wilderness for safety (Revelation 12:14), an angel brings the Gospel by flying (Revelation 14:6), and birds fly to participate in God's feast (Revelation 19:17). The word is used each time to express free movement in the air, often related to supernatural or eschatological events.
G4072.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us of the power and freedom of celestial creatures that fulfill the divine will. The angels that fly symbolize agility and quick obedience to God's mission, while the woman who flies shows how God protects His people by removing them from threat. It is an image of hope: even in the face of chaos, there is a heavenly refuge offered by the power of God.

sens: Mass of solid and fixed stone, forming a mountain or cliff
Natural cavity carved in the rock
Cornerstone symbolizing a stable and unshakeable foundation
Spiritual base or indestructible founding principle
G4073.detail:
1. The rock is a large mass of natural, raw, and unshakeable stone, contrasting with a simple detached stone. When Jesus speaks of building a house on the rock (Matthew 7:24), he evokes this solidity: a foundation so firm that no storm can shake it. The tomb of Christ is hewn from the rock (Matthew 27:60), using the density and permanence of the stone to protect a grave.
2. The rock also designates a natural cavity or cave, a protection carved into the mountain. Revelation describes men hiding in the rocks and caves, seeking refuge (Revelation 6:15-16).
3. In symbolic language, the rock becomes the image of absolute solidity and indestructibility. When Jesus says, "You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church" (Matthew 16:18), he uses an image of an unshakeable foundation, promising that nothing will be able to destroy what he builds.
4. For Paul, the spiritual rock of the desert is Christ himself (1 Corinthians 10:4): the rock that accompanies Israel and provides living water is an image of Christ as the source of eternal life and sustenance.
G4073.origine: The Greek word petra comes from a root that designates a natural, raw, and unshakeable rocky mass. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew word sela, which evokes both the rock and the protective cavity carved into the mountain. The Latin word petra has the same origin. The distinction between petra (the mass of rock) and petros (a detached stone) is important: petra emphasizes solidity and permanence, while petros refers to a stone that can be grasped and moved. This difference sheds light on why the New Testament plays on these two words when it speaks of Peter and the foundational stone.
G4073.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the provided usages, mainly in Matthew and Luke, in contexts where solidity or protection is decisive. Matthew uses it for the parable of the house built on the rock (7:24-25) and for the promise to Peter (16:18), then for the tomb of Christ (27:60). Luke takes up the parable of the solid foundation (6:48) and the image of the barren rock in the parable of the sower (8:13). In 1 Corinthians 10:4, Paul uses petra figuratively: the rock of the desert that gives water is spiritually Christ. In these passages, petra designates both a geographical or material reality (a mountain, a cavity, a tomb) and a spiritual image (the foundation of the Church, the source of life in Christ).
G4073.portee: For the believer, this word invites one to build their life on an unshakeable foundation: not on the shifting sand of circumstances or passions, but on the teaching of Jesus and the solidity of the Church that he builds. The image of the rock also speaks to those who feel fragile or in danger: the rock offers refuge, protection, stability. Finally, by seeing Christ as the spiritual rock that nourishes, one discovers that he is not a dead and mineral foundation, but a living, present source of life for all who drink from him by faith.

sens: Apostle of Jesus, disciple of John the Baptist who became the leader of the twelve
One of the three privileged witnesses of the Transfiguration and the Garden of Gethsemane
The disciple who confesses Jesus as Messiah and receives the keys to the Kingdom
The one who denies Jesus three times before His resurrection
The preacher and healer in the early days of the Church in Jerusalem
G4074G.detail:
1. Peter (whose Aramaic name is Cephas, "rock") is a fisherman from Galilee, brother of Andrew, whom Jesus calls to be His disciple by the sea: "Simon, called Peter" (Matthew 4:18). He becomes one of the twelve apostles and one of the three closest to Jesus, along with James and John.
2. He witnesses major events in the life of Jesus: the Transfiguration on the mountain (Luke 9:28), the agony in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:37), and the resurrection that the women announce to him first (Luke 24:12).
3. At Caesarea Philippi, he confesses Jesus: "You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God" (Matthew 16:16), and Jesus tells him: "You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church" (Matthew 16:18), giving him special authority.
4. Despite his declared faith, he denies Jesus three times during the trial, fulfilling the warning that Jesus had given him (Luke 22:54-62).
5. After Pentecost, Peter becomes the leader and spokesperson of the apostles: he preaches to the crowd on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:38), performs healings, and plays a central role in the beginnings of the Church in Jerusalem.
G4074G.origine: The name Πέτρος comes from the Greek πέτρα (petra), which means "rock" or "stone." In Aramaic, he is called Κηφᾶς (Cephas), which has exactly the same meaning. Jesus gave this new name to Simon in reference to his future solidity and his role in building the Church, playing on the image of the stone: a stable and unshakeable rock. This name reflects his apostolic vocation.
G4074G.emploi: Peter appears 153 times in the New Testament, more than any other apostle. He is mentioned in all the Gospels and plays a central role in Acts: a disciple personally called by Jesus (Matthew 4:18), he is gradually trained during the earthly ministry, knows the glory of the Transfiguration but also the humiliation of denial. After the resurrection, he becomes the leader of the Church in Jerusalem, preaching, healing, and making major community decisions (Acts 2:38, 10:13). The Epistle of James and that of John also contain letters attributed to Peter. His portrait in the Gospels is nuanced: faithful but weak, courageous but also fearful, overwhelmed by the depth of the Word but always returning to Jesus.
G4074G.portee: Peter is the model of the realistic disciple: not a flawless hero, but an ordinary man whom Jesus calls, whom Jesus slowly transforms, and who ultimately becomes a powerful instrument despite his failures. His denial and restoration show that unfaithfulness does not nullify God's call. His transition from fear to bold proclamation invites every reader to recognize that the resurrection changes everything and that the Holy Spirit gives the strength to witness.

sens: Containing stones or rock
Having little soil depth due to underlying rock
Figuratively: receiving the Word without lasting roots
G4075.detail:
1. The word literally describes land covered with stones or composed of rock. It is the opposite of fertile and cultivated land.
2. In the parable of the sower, it specifically refers to shallow soil, where the rock comes close to the surface. The seed sprouts quickly, deceived by the superficial moisture, but without roots to survive (Matthew 13:5, Mark 4:5).
3. Jesus applies this image to the heart that receives the Word with initial joy but without deep conversion: enthusiasm fades as soon as trial comes (Matthew 13:20, Mark 4:16). This serves as a warning about the fragility of superficial faith.
G4075.origine: The word comes from "stone" (πέτρα, petra) and "form" or "appearance" (εἶδος, eidos): literally "having the form of stone," "resembling stone." It is an adjective formed to express a rocky or stony quality. The word designates not only scattered pebbles but a continuous layer of rock that prevents rooting.
G4075.emploi: The word appears only four times in the New Testament, exclusively in the parable of the sower in Matthew and Mark. It occurs in two contexts: first to physically describe the terrain (Matthew 13:5 and Mark 4:5), and then to symbolically identify listeners who welcome the Word without depth (Matthew 13:20 and Mark 4:16). Jesus uses this familiar figure to His listeners — every farmer knows a stony field — to teach a spiritual truth: a faith without roots does not survive.
G4075.portee: This image invites the believer to examine the depth of their own conversion. Receiving the Word with joy is just a beginning; what matters is that it takes root in a worked, transformed heart, available for suffering and renunciation. The term warns us against the illusion of a surface faith, appealing at the moment but incapable of bearing lasting fruit.

sens: Aromatic herb with small leaves
Herb cultivated and used in Jewish purification rites
G4076.detail:
1. Wormwood is an herb with small, divided leaves, known for its strong odor and bitter taste. It grows in a Mediterranean climate and was commonly cultivated in ancient Middle Eastern gardens.
2. The Jews of Jesus' time included wormwood among the fine herbs that were to be tithed to the Temple, as shown in Luke 11:42. Jesus criticizes the Pharisees who meticulously observe this tax obligation on insignificant herbs but forget the much more important commandments: justice and love for God.
G4076.origine: The Greek word πήγανον (pēganon) designates common wormwood, cultivated since antiquity in the Mediterranean. In Hebrew, this plant is called פִּגָם (pigam). The Greek word does not vary based on context: it simply names this plant well-known to the inhabitants of the Mediterranean basin.
G4076.emploi: Wormwood appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 11:42, during Jesus' discourse against the Pharisees and the teachers of the Law. Jesus mentions it as an example of an herb subject to tithing according to strict rabbinic practice. This concrete detail illustrates Jesus' reproach: the religious leaders who are scrupulous in small matters neglect the true requirements of God.
G4076.portee: This word reminds us that formal piety — tithing on every herb in the garden — can become a caricature of true obedience if it obscures love and justice. For the Christian reader, it serves as a lesson on the danger of privileging outward observance at the expense of the heart.

sens: Point d'où jaillit l'eau naturellement
Puits ou réservoir d'eau
Écoulement ou flux de liquide du corps
Origine, principe d'où procède quelque chose
Pourvoyeur ou principe intarissable
G4077.detail:
1. A source is the natural point from which water springs from the ground: it is the living origin of a watercourse. In John 4:6, Jacob's well is a source that provides water.
2. The word also refers to a well or a reservoir fed by an underground source — a place where one draws water (John 4:6: Jesus sits by Jacob's well).
3. In Mark 5:29, a woman suffering from a hemorrhage sees this flow stop: the source here is an involuntary flow of blood that had emptied from her body.
4. Metaphorically, a source is the principle or origin from which something proceeds. In John 4:14, the water that Jesus gives becomes "a spring of water welling up" — it generates a new life that never runs dry.
5. In James 3:11, the question "Does a spring pour forth from the same opening fresh and bitter water?" treats the source as a principle that produces and reveals what comes from it: a moral or inner source generates what it lets escape. 2 Peter 2:17 calls certain men "wells without water" — appearances of a source that deliver nothing living.
G4077.origine: The Greek word πηγή (pēgē) comes from a root evoking the springing forth and pouring out. In Hebrew, it primarily translates עַיִן (source, eye) and מָקוֹר (source, origin). The image is that of water flowing out of itself, flowing continuously — hence the extended meaning to anything that produces, generates, or continuously provides.
G4077.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the New Testament, mostly in John and Revelation. In Mark 5:29 and James 3:11-12, it is purely physical: flow of blood or gushing water. But John and Revelation use it spiritually: in John 4:14, the water given by Jesus is a source that wells up to eternal life — it symbolizes the Spirit and the new life that never runs dry. 2 Peter 2:17 reverses the image: false teachers are "wells without water," empty promises. Revelation speaks of the spring of life (7:17, 21:6), a place of fullness and eternal rest.
G4077.portee: This word invites the believer to recognize in Jesus and His Spirit the living source for which he thirsts — not stagnant or depleting water, but a continuous spring of life. It also warns: what comes from a man's heart reveals his deep nature, just as a source reveals its quality by what it produces. Seeking true sources (the Word, the Spirit) rather than false ones (false teachers, false wisdom) is a matter of spiritual life or death.

sens: Ériger une structure, notamment une tente, de manière ferme et stable
Établir ou fonder quelque chose de manière durable
G4078.detail:
1. The word evokes the action of erecting a tent or a structure: it is firmly fixed to the ground so that it stands upright and does not collapse. In Hebrews 8:2, this is how the Lord has "erected" the true heavenly tabernacle — not in a temporary or fragile manner, but established firmly and permanently.
2. Figuratively, "to erect" means to found, institute, or set up something stable and durable. This is why this verb is suitable for speaking of the establishment of the divine tabernacle: it is not built by human hands, but constituted and strengthened by God Himself in an unshakeable manner.
G4078.origine: The verb πήγνυμι comes from a root that expresses the idea of fixing, making solid and immobile. In biblical Hebrew, it is mostly encountered as a translation of נָטָה (to stretch) and תָּקַע (to plant, to drive in), both of which denote the action of erecting a tent or firmly fixing something in the ground. This image of stability and foundation is key: to erect is to make fixed and durable.
G4078.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 8:2. In this passage, the Apostle Paul asserts that Jesus ministers in the "true tabernacle" that the Lord has erected — not an earthly tabernacle built by human hands, but the heavenly tabernacle established by God Himself. This liturgical and theological context emphasizes that what is erected by God possesses a solidity, legitimacy, and durability that no one can match.
G4078.portee: This word reminds the believer that Christ's work in the heavenly sanctuary rests on a divine foundation, not a human one. The tabernacle "erected" by the Lord means that our access to God and our salvation do not depend on our fragile efforts, but on what God Himself has established in an unshakeable manner. It is a word of trust and stability for faith.

sens: Dispositif de direction d'un navire, fixé à l'arrière de la coque
Au figuré : instrument de commande qui oriente une direction ou un comportement
G4079.detail:
1. The rudder is the movable part that allows a ship to change direction. It is a submerged blade fixed at the back of the boat, controlled by the helmsman to steer the course of the vessel. James 3:4 compares a small rudder directing a large ship driven by fierce winds: despite the enormity of the ship and the strength of the winds, this tiny instrument remains master of its trajectory.
2. Figuratively, the rudder symbolizes anything that controls or directs a larger whole. James uses it to speak of the tongue: it is like a rudder that, although small, directs the entire body and even the deep intentions of a person, for good or for evil.
G4079.origine: The Greek word comes from πηδός (pedos), the blade or oar, the instrument that pushes the water. The rudder operates on the same principle: it is a submerged blade oriented to steer the boat. The term specifically designates this small blade that, by its position, influences the direction of a much larger whole.
G4079.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, each time in relation to actual or figurative marine direction. In Acts 27:40, it refers to the rudder (in the plural: "rudders") of a distressed ship trying to reach the shore despite the storm: this is the concrete and technical usage. In James 3:4, it illustrates the power of the human tongue to steer an entire person, just as the rudder directs a giant ship. The image remains that of a small instrument capable of mastering a force much greater than itself.
G4079.portee: The rudder teaches the Christian that small things can have an outsized influence. The tongue, though small, shapes our entire life and that of others. This image invites vigilance: how to steer our inner "rudder" — our words, our choices — so that our life, like a well-guided ship, is not cast adrift by the storms of this world?

sens: Of what size, of what dimension?
What importance, what weight?
Expressing admiration for greatness or excellence
G4080.detail:
1. The word raises a question about the physical dimension or magnitude of something: "See with what large letters I have written to you" (Galatians 6:11) — Paul emphasizes the impressive size of the letters he has written by hand, likely to highlight the importance of his message or due to vision problems.
2. It applies to personal greatness, weight, or importance of a person: "How great is the man to whom Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth of the spoils" (Hebrews 7:4) — the question concerns the superiority and excellence of Melchizedek, who received tithes from Abraham.
3. In both cases, the word expresses wonder or emphasis: it does not simply describe a dimension but invites the reader to measure for themselves and recognize the greatness or importance of what is presented.
G4080.origine: πηλίκος comes from an interrogative root and literally means "of what magnitude." It is an interrogative adjective, related to words that pose questions about quantity. In the Greek Old Testament, it sometimes translates כָּמַהּ ("how much," "as"). The word belongs to the class of interrogatives that invite reflection or comparison.
G4080.emploi: Πηλίκος appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the context of questions or exclamations that ask the reader to evaluate a greatness. In Galatians 6:11, Paul uses it to draw attention to the size of the letters of his personal writing, which serves to show the importance of the message he signs. In Hebrews 7:4, the author poses a rhetorical question about the greatness of Melchizedek to establish his superiority over Abraham — and thus over the Levitical priesthood of which Abraham is the ancestor. In both cases, πηλίκος functions as a pedagogical tool to engage the reader in reflection.
G4080.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian faith is not a passive adherence but an invitation to "see" and "consider" — to take the time to measure for oneself the greatness of what God offers. In Hebrews 7, this pushes the reader to recognize the excellence of Christ's priesthood compared to the old covenant. In Galatians 6, it emphasizes Paul's personal commitment to his apostleship.

sens: Soft and pliable material that the potter shapes to make vessels
Wet, moist earth, a mixture of soil and water
Image of the weakness and fragility of the creature in the hands of the Creator
G4081.detail:
1. Strictly speaking, mud or clay is the raw material of the potter. It is a malleable earth that the potter can shape at will to make different kinds of vessels, useful or not (Romans 9:21). This image shows the power of the creator who shapes what is inert.

2. More concretely, it is mud in the ordinary sense: soaked earth, a wet paste. This is exactly what Jesus does by spitting on the ground and applying this mud to the eyes of the blind man (John 9:6). The gesture carries a creative power: this is ordinary mud transformed into an instrument of healing.

3. Spiritually, mud or clay symbolizes the condition of the creature: fragile, without inherent substance, entirely dependent on the one who formed it. It reminds us that we are "dust," as the Old Testament affirms, and that our value comes only from our Creator.
G4081.origine: The Greek word pēlos refers to mud or clay, the raw material of the potter. It generally translates in the Greek Old Testament the Hebrew "homèr" (חֹמֶר), which literally means the potter's clay, and also "tit" (טִיט), mud or mire. The root evokes the idea of plasticity, malleability: it is a material that can be shaped. The image of the potter shaping the clay is ancient in the East and carries great theological weight: it expresses the absolute power of the creator over creation.
G4081.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the New Testament, concentrated in two key passages. First, it refers to the mud that Jesus makes by spitting on the ground (John 9:6, 11, 14, 15) to heal the blind man on the Sabbath. This mud is not a magical ingredient: it expresses the creative act of Jesus, who uses simple elements to restore what is broken, and who deliberately transgresses the Sabbath law. Then, in Romans 9:21, Paul uses "clay" in the literal sense for the famous image of the potter: God has the absolute right to make from the same lump (humanity, Israel) vessels of honor or ordinary vessels. The word shifts from the concrete sense (the material) to the theological sense (the fragility of the creature).
G4081.portee: This word invites the Christian to meditate on two essential truths. First, Jesus is the master of creation: he can transform what seems inert or corrupted into an instrument of salvation and restoration. Second, we ourselves are clay in the hands of the divine Potter: this fragility is not a humiliation, but an opportunity to discover that our value comes entirely from the one who has shaped us and who continues to transform us. The mud applied to the blind eyes is also a promise: our weakness is the place where God's power is manifested.

sens: Small leather bag for carrying provisions or travel items
Traveler's or beggar's satchel
Purse or alms (figurative sense)
G4082.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a small leather bag that travelers carried with them to hold food or other belongings. When Jesus sends his disciples on a mission, he instructs them to take nothing with them, not even a sack (Luke 9:3), so that their trust rests solely on God and the hospitality of others.
2. It is also the typical bag carried by beggars or vagabonds to collect alms or survive on the roads. In the context of mission sending, refusing the sack means adopting total simplicity: the disciples must live off the generosity of others, just as Jesus himself did.
3. The word can more broadly evoke a purse or a place where one keeps their belongings, hence its connection to money and material resources. When Jesus tells his disciples to take a sack from now on (Luke 22:36), after his resurrection, he acknowledges that they will need to provide for their material needs in a normal way.
G4082.origine: The Greek word pēra comes from the idea of a soft, worked leather object, suitable for holding. It is a simple and concrete word that designates a common utensil of the ancient daily life. It appears in other Greek texts to describe the belongings of travelers and the poor. In Aramaic and biblical Hebrew, there is no exact traditional equivalent, as the Greek word captures a reality of the Hellenistic Greco-Roman world.
G4082.emploi: The word appears six times in the Gospels, always in contexts of mission. Matthew, Mark, and Luke report Jesus' instructions to his disciples before sending them out two by two to preach and heal. The absence of a sack symbolizes detachment from material possessions and trust in God. After the resurrection (Luke 22:36), Jesus modifies his instruction: from now on, the disciples can and should take what is necessary with them, including a purse and a sack, thus recognizing that ordinary life requires provisions. This change marks the transition between the extraordinary mission during Jesus' earthly life and the normal ministry of the Church.
G4082.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the relationship to material goods. Jesus' initial command teaches that voluntary poverty and trust in God open the heart to his providence. But the later permission to carry a sack shows that God does not require permanent asceticism: it is enough not to make wealth our idol. For the Christian disciple, it is a lesson in balance between trust in God and responsible management of resources.

sens: Forearm, from the elbow to the hand
Ancient unit of length, about 45 centimeters
Measure of height or distance
Extended or added duration
G4083.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the forearm, from the elbow joint to the hand — the part of the body that one naturally extends to measure a distance. This concrete image of the arm gave rise to the unit of measurement.
2. A cubit is a unit of length, very common in antiquity: it is roughly equivalent to the length of a forearm, about 45 to 50 centimeters depending on the peoples and eras. It is an "anthropomorphic" measure, meaning based on the human body.
3. In Revelation, the cubit is used to measure the heavenly wall: "He measured the wall, and found one hundred and forty-four cubits" (Revelation 21:17). It serves as a concrete standard of length to express dimensions.
4. In Matthew and Luke, "adding a cubit to the length of one's life" uses the word figuratively: it confuses the act of measuring a length with that of prolonging time. The cubit then becomes a portion of life, however minuscule — one cannot extend a bit by worry.
G4083.origine: The word comes from the Greek root that expresses the idea of "bending" or "flexing" — the forearm being the limb that bends at the elbow. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it almost always translates אַמָּה (ammah), the Hebrew word for cubit, which has the same etymology and meaning. This word, very common in descriptions of the temple and the ark, was familiar to all speakers of the ancient Near East.
G4083.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, always in contexts of measurement or dimension. Two occurrences in Matthew and Luke aim to express insignificance: "adding a cubit to the length of one's life" means that we cannot, through our worries, prolong even a moment of our existence (Matthew 6:27; Luke 12:25) — it is a hyperbole where the cubit symbolizes a tiny portion of time. In John, it measures a real distance: the disciples approach about two hundred cubits from the shore with their net of fish (John 21:8). In Revelation, it becomes the unit of cosmic measurement for the heavenly wall and its twelve gates (Revelation 21:17), reminding us that even the dimensions of heaven can be expressed in human terms.
G4083.portee: This measure reminds us that God speaks to humans in a language they understand — that of their bodies and daily tools. It also teaches us humility: we cannot extend our life by a single cubit through our anxieties (Matthew 6:27; Luke 12:25). And it reveals that heaven itself conforms to a proportion that man can grasp — heaven is not without measure, but intelligible (Revelation 21:17).

sens: to take someone or something with the hand or by force
to seize someone to stop or capture them
to catch fish or game
G4084.detail:
1. Seize primarily means to take or catch something with the hand. It is the concrete gesture of one who grasps: in Acts 3:7, Peter "seizes" the right hand of the lame man to raise him up, which is an act of physical and benevolent taking.
2. The word also refers to seizing someone, capturing them to stop them. This is the dominant meaning in the Gospel of John: the authorities seek to "seize" Jesus (John 7:30, 7:44, 10:39), meaning to make him a prisoner. In 2 Corinthians 11:32, a governor wants to "seize" Paul to arrest him.
3. In the context of fishing or hunting, the word means to catch: in John 21:3, the disciples "caught nothing" that night — they did not catch any fish.
G4084.origine: The Greek word piazō is related to piézō, which literally means "to press" or "to squeeze." It is a late verb, but very common in New Testament Greek and late Greek in general. It evokes the fundamental idea of seizing, taking by force or action, hence its use in the Greek Old Testament to translate the Hebrew 'âkhaz (אָחַז), which also means "to take" or "to seize."
G4084.emploi: This verb appears 12 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospel of John (7 occurrences) and in Acts. In John, it mainly designates the attempt of the Jewish authorities to arrest Jesus during his earthly life: it is a verb of hostility, of threat. In Acts, it retains this sense of arrest (Acts 12:4, 2 Corinthians 11:32) or takes on the factual sense of capture or taking (John 21:3, 21:10 for fishing). In Revelation 19:20, it refers to the capture of the Beast. The word always expresses an action of effectively seizing, without weakness or failure.
G4084.portee: This verb reminds us that Jesus could not be arrested before the hour of God: although his enemies wanted to "seize" him, no one could lay a hand on him until the appointed time (John 7:30). It is an affirmation of divine sovereignty over the destiny of Christ. For the disciple, the word also teaches that our trust does not depend on the power of men, but on God's plan that controls all events.

sens: to press hard on something to compress it
to pack a substance by pressing to increase its density
to reduce in volume by applying pressure
G4085.detail:
1. The verb πιέζω means properly "to press hard" or "to compress": it is to apply pressure on an object to reduce it, pack it, or densify it. In Luke 6:38, the measure poured into the donor's bosom is "pressed down," meaning packed and compressed by pressure, to contain more grain in the same volume.
2. By extension, the action of "pressing" can refer to tightly squeezing something to embrace or hold it, an image of cohesion and fullness: the measure "pressed down, shaken together, and running over" evokes an abundance so pressed that it cannot be contained.
3. More generally, this word expresses the intensity of an action that is exerted with force: it is to compress, condense, make dense and compact.
G4085.origine: The verb πιέζω comes from a Greek root expressing the idea of "pressing" or "packing." It is related to other Greek verbs describing actions of compression. In the Septuagint, it translates the Hebrew דָּרַךְ (darak, "to tread upon," "to trample") in Micah 6:15, showing that the basic meaning is that of pressure exerted by weight or force.
G4085.emploi: The verb πιέζω appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 6:38. Jesus uses this word to describe how a generous measure of grains or provisions is poured into a person's garment (the bosom): not only poured, but "pressed down," meaning packed, compressed to maximize the quantity. This context of divine generosity in response to human generosity emphasizes that God does not give sparingly, but with an abundance so pressed that it overflows.
G4085.portee: This word reminds the believer that generosity towards others does not go unanswered: God returns a hundredfold, and even "with interest," a measure so full that it overflows. The image of grain pressed down to overflowing symbolizes a grace that exceeds all expectation and human measure.

sens: Words designed to please and convince by their appearance rather than by their solidity
Arguments based on what seems probable or plausible, without true evidence
Eloquence aimed at persuading rather than demonstrating the truth
G4086.detail:
1. The word refers to a type of skillfully constructed speech intended to seduce the listener and persuade them, relying on what appears pleasant or credible. It is a language that shines through its forms, elegance, or apparent logic, without necessarily resting on solid demonstration. In Colossians 2:4, Paul warns against these "seductive speeches" used by false teachers to mislead Christians, deceiving them with words that sound good but lead away from the truth of Christ.

2. The background of the word evokes the contrast between two ways of convincing: the "probable" or "plausible" arguments, which play on appearance and superficial adherence, and the true demonstration, which is based on certain foundations. A seductive speech is not lacking in order or logic, but it sacrifices solidity for persuasive effect — which is why it easily deceives those who do not discern.
G4086.origine: The Greek word comes from πιθανός (pithanós), meaning "persuasive, plausible, probable," and the noun -λογία (logia), "speech, word." The root πιθ- evokes the idea of persuasion and apparent credibility. Ancient Greeks already opposed this type of argumentation (based on plausibility) to ἀπόδειξις (apódeixis), meaning certain and irrefutable demonstration. It is a term of eloquence and rhetoric, recalling the concern of speakers to seduce through form as much as through content.
G4086.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Colossians 2:4. Paul uses it to warn the Christians in Colossae against the sophists and false teachers who threaten their faith. The latter use smooth and persuasive words — a "seductive speech" — to divert them from communion with Christ. The apostle places this warning at the heart of his struggle against heresy: it is necessary to recognize that the danger does not only come from false ideas, but from the way they are presented, with a speaking art that fascinates and deceives.
G4086.portee: This word calls Christians to vigilance: not to confuse the beauty of words with the truth of the Gospel. Paul teaches us that faith must be rooted in the solidity of Christ, not in human eloquence, even if refined. It is an invitation to develop spiritual discernment — to listen not only to what is said, but how it is said and whether it is truly grounded in the Word of God.

sens: To become or make bitter in taste
To experience or cause an unpleasant, bitter sensation in the mouth or stomach
To become embittered, hostile, or bitter in one's heart toward someone
To transform something sweet into something of bitterness and pain
G4087.detail:
1. The most direct sense is that of taste: to make bitter, to give an unpleasant and acrid flavor. In Revelation, a star called Wormwood falls from heaven and changes the waters into wormwood, making them bitter (Revelation 8:11). The little book that John must swallow will first be sweet in the mouth, but then bitter in the stomach (Revelation 10:9 and 10:10).
2. The word also describes an unpleasant physical experience: that of tasting or absorbing something that provokes disgust or repulsion. Swallowing the little book, John first feels honey, then suddenly bitterness fills his stomach (Revelation 10:10).
3. Figuratively, the word means to become embittered or bitter emotionally toward a person, particularly in relationships. Paul exhorts husbands not to be bitter, meaning not to become hostile or resentful toward their wives (Colossians 3:19).
4. More broadly, it is to transform a good into misfortune: what could have been beneficial or pleasant becomes a source of pain and inner suffering.
G4087.origine: The word comes from the adjective πικρός (bitter, sour in taste, or figuratively, harsh, hostile, painful). The root expresses the idea of something that stings, that assaults the senses. In Hebrew, the word is often close to מָרַד (to revolt, to embitter) or קָצַף (to become angry). The family of πικρός also includes the notion of physical and moral bitterness, of harshness in relationships.
G4087.emploi: The verb appears four times in the New Testament, mainly in Revelation and once in Paul. In Revelation, it describes the action of literally making bitter (the waters by wormwood, or the little book from the taste of honey to bitterness): it is a mysterious and symbolic transformation that affects John during his vision. In Paul (Colossians 3:19), the word takes on a moral and relational dimension: it is about not allowing frustration or anger to embitter one's heart toward one's wife, not to cultivate a bitterness that would poison marital love. The contrast between sweet and bitter in Revelation illustrates how a revelation can first be comforting, then become painful to assimilate.
G4087.portee: This word reminds us that our feelings can become bitter, that resentment poisons the most intimate relationships. Paul's warning to husbands invites each one to examine their heart: let us guard against allowing bitterness to arise and grow that would harden our bonds with those we love. In Revelation, the honey that becomes bitterness also speaks of the complexity of God's mystery: what seems sweet to receive may require from us a difficult and painful transformation.

sens: Acrid and unpleasant taste, opposed to sweetness
Disposition of the heart characterized by resentment, malice, or hatred
Deep-seated hostility that poisons relationships
Feeling that spreads and contaminates those around
G4088.detail:
1. Bitterness primarily denotes the acrid and repulsive taste of certain substances: it is the opposite of sweetness. It is a physical sensation, but also a powerful image to describe what is repugnant.

2. In moral and spiritual terms, bitterness is a disposition of the heart characterized by resentment, hostility, or malice toward others. In Acts 8:23, Peter describes Simon as being "in the gall of bitterness": Simon is filled with a malice that poisons him from within. It is a moral poisoning.

3. Bitterness can become a general attitude, a negative state of mind: in Ephesians 4:31, Paul exhorts Christians to let "all bitterness" disappear, alongside anger and slander. It manifests in the way one speaks and acts (Romans 3:14: "Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness").

4. Bitterness is also a "root" that produces shoots and contaminates those around (Hebrews 12:15). Like a weed, it takes root in the heart and spreads, infecting many people around.
G4088.origine: The Greek word pikría comes from the adjective pikrós ("bitter, sour"), which originally denotes the acrid and unpleasant taste. In Hebrew, the Old Testament primarily uses the word mar ("bitter") to express this idea. The Greek word has retained the image of taste to describe a reality of the heart: just as bitter taste repulses and hurts the tongue, moral bitterness repulses and hurts the soul. It is a natural metaphor in biblical language.
G4088.emploi: The word bitterness appears four times in the New Testament, always in a moral or spiritual context. It is never used to describe a simple taste in the physical sense, but always to paint a state of the heart or soul. In Acts 8:23, it characterizes the spiritual corruption of Simon the magician. In Romans 3:14 and Ephesians 4:31, it describes an attitude of malice expressed through speech (cursing, anger, slander). In Hebrews 12:15, bitterness is presented as an underground root: initially hidden, it grows and ultimately poisons an entire community. Each time, bitterness is presented as something to be rejected and eradicated from Christian life.
G4088.portee: Bitterness is a spiritual poison that corrupts the one who nourishes it and contaminates those around them. The Bible does not minimize its destructive power: a single root of bitterness can infect many people and disturb an entire assembly. For the Christian, the word calls for vigilance of the heart: to examine one's feelings, to forgive rather than harbor resentment, and to cultivate the grace of God which alone can heal this inner wound. It is an invitation to the transformation of the heart.

sens: Having a harsh, unpleasant taste, opposite of sweet
Causing pain or suffering; harsh, violent
Revealing a resentful hostility or envious jealousy
G4089.detail:
1. In its most direct sense, bitter qualifies what has an unpleasant and harsh taste — the opposite of sweet or soft. This is the physical sense of the word: a spring can produce bitter water just as it produces sweet water (James 3:11).

2. By extension, bitter describes what hurts or causes pain, not in taste but in the soul: a bitter word, a bitter experience. It is a moral or emotional harshness.

3. When the Bible speaks of bitter zeal (James 3:14), it refers to an envious and resentful jealousy, an ambition that poisons the heart — a passion that, like the bitterness of taste, leaves a toxic aftertaste and troubles everything it touches.
G4089.origine: The Greek word pikros comes from a very ancient root that describes the idea of pricking or piercing. Bitterness, like a point, hurts the tongue and the heart. In Hebrew, the word mar (מַר) conveys the same idea: what is bitter, sharp, cutting. The family of the Greek word includes other forms that express sharpness or pain. The common image is that of a sharp attack, whether sensory or moral.
G4089.emploi: The word bitter appears twice in the New Testament, both times in James. First in James 3:11, where it describes the bitter water of a spring, in a rhetorical question about nature: can sweet and bitter water come from the same spring? The context suggests that it is impossible — a spring produces only one type of water. Then in James 3:14, bitter qualifies an envious and contentious zeal: it is not a pure zeal directed toward God, but a bitter jealousy that germinates in the heart and corrupts everything. In both cases, bitterness is a poison, something that should not mix with purity.
G4089.portee: For the Christian, this word invites personal examination. Just as a spring cannot give both sweet and bitter water, a regenerated soul cannot mix jealousy and praise of God, envy and charity. Bitter reminds us that our hidden motivations — pride, rivalry, resentment — are poisons that corrupt our spiritual life and testimony. It is a call to heart purity.

sens: In a way that tastes or feels bitterness
With intense pain or sorrow
With tears and deep remorse
G4090.detail: 1. The word first describes a physical sensation of bitterness in taste, like what is bitter on the palate — but in the Bible, it is always used figuratively. 2. It denotes deep suffering, an intense moral pain that overwhelms the one who feels it. 3. In the two biblical uses provided, Peter wept "bitterly" after denying Jesus (Matthew 26:75 and Luke 22:62): these were not ordinary tears, but the expression of extreme sorrow, an inner rupture in the face of his betrayal.
G4090.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective "pikros" (bitter), which evokes the repulsive taste of what is bitter. The root refers to the physical image of bitterness — an unpleasant taste — which has extended to describe moral suffering. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the Greek word often translates "mar" or its derivatives, which express bitterness both in the literal sense (a bitter drink) and in the figurative sense (a bitter affliction).
G4090.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the account of Peter's denial. Matthew 26:75 and Luke 22:62 describe the same moment: after denying Jesus three times, Peter went out and wept "bitterly." It is a tear of deep repentance, not of mere superficial regret. The use of the Greek word emphasizes the intensity of his suffering and remorse for what he has done.
G4090.portee: This word reveals the reality of authentic repentance. Peter's bitter tears are not a mere softening of heart: they mark a conversion of the heart, a sincere pain over the wrong committed. For the reader, this shows that even after a serious fall, deep and honest repentance opens a path to restoration — Peter, who wept bitterly, will become the apostle on whom Jesus will build His Church.

sens: Roman governor of Judea
The one who condemned Jesus to death
The representative of civil power in the face of Jewish religious authority
G4091.detail:
1. Pilate is the Roman governor (prefect) of the province of Judea under the reign of Tiberius. Matthew presents him as "Pontius Pilate, the governor" (Matthew 27:2), an official title that indicates his administrative and judicial authority over the territory.

2. Pilate is the one who, after questioning Jesus, yielded to the pressures of the Jewish authorities and the crowd to condemn Jesus to crucifixion. John reports his direct dialogue with Jesus: "Pilate said to Him: Are You not speaking to me? Do You not know that I have the power to crucify You?" (John 19:10), revealing both his authority and his hesitation in the face of Jesus' innocence.

3. Pilate embodies the conflict between Roman political power and Jewish religious authority. Luke shows how he sent Jesus to Herod, and then the two worked together against Christ: "Herod, with his soldiers, treated Him with contempt... he sent Him back to Pilate" (Luke 23:11), illustrating the power struggles of the time.
G4091.origine: Pilate is a Latin name, Pontius Pilatus, where Pontius is the nickname (cognomen) of his family and Pilatus likely means "armed with a javelin" (pilon in Latin). He was historically the Roman prefect of Judea from 26 to 36 AD, appointed by the governor of Syria. His name appears 53 times in the New Testament, almost always in the context of the Passion of Jesus.
G4091.emploi: Pilate appears 53 times in the New Testament, concentrated in the Passion narratives (Matthew 27, Mark 15, Luke 23, John 18-19) and a few references in Acts and 1 Timothy. In the Gospels, he is always presented as the one who officially holds the power to judge Jesus and decide His fate. Matthew emphasizes his symbolic act of washing his hands: "Pilate... washed his hands" (Matthew 27:24), showing his desire to absolve himself of responsibility. John highlights the direct exchanges between Jesus and Pilate, revealing Pilate's awareness of Jesus' innocence despite his political weakness. In Acts 3:13, Peter reminds the crowd: "God glorified His servant Jesus, whom you delivered and denied before Pilate" (Acts 3:13), placing Pilate in the apostolic narrative of collective guilt. In 1 Timothy 6:13, Jesus "testified before Pontius Pilate to the good confession," recalling Jesus before His judge.
G4091.portee: Pilate represents for the believer the fragility of earthly power in the face of truth: although he held Roman authority, he yielded to pressure. His story raises questions about moral courage and responsibility before justice: yielding to lies or the crowd despite knowing what is right. It also shows that even the most powerful political authority of the time could not thwart the divine plan of salvation.

sens: to swell, to become swollen (referring to a part of the body)
to increase in volume due to swelling or inflammation
G4092.detail:
1. The verb "to swell" describes the swelling or tumefaction of a part of the body, a visible increase in volume. In Acts 28:6, after a serpent bites Paul, the inhabitants of Malta expect his arm or body to "swell" — the usual reaction to a venomous bite — but nothing happens, which astonishes them and leads them to recognize Paul as a being protected by the gods.
2. In a broader sense, the term refers to any process of swelling, inflammation, or enlargement, whether due to an injury, a sting, an illness, or another cause.
G4092.origine: The verb πίμπρημι (pimprēmi) is infrequent in classical Greek prose. It derives from a root expressing the idea of swelling or distension. The word is primarily used in the Greek version of the Old Testament (the Septuagint) to translate Hebrew terms denoting swelling, notably צָבֶה (tsavé) in the texts of Numbers concerning curses and trials. It is a concrete and descriptive word, painting the image of a body affected by a visible physical condition.
G4092.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 28:6, during Paul's shipwreck in Malta. The context is dramatic: after coming out of the sea, Paul gathers wood for the fire when a serpent escapes from the branches and bites him. The pagan inhabitants, accustomed to the consequences of venomous bites, naturally expect Paul to "swell" quickly and then die. However, against all odds, Paul suffers no harm. This absence of swelling becomes proof, in the eyes of these islanders, of the divine protection exercised over the apostle, marking a decisive turning point in their attitude towards him.
G4092.portee: This humble yet concrete word reminds us that God's protection often manifests in visible and tangible ways: it can be seen, it can be observed, it astonishes. The absence of swelling in Paul, in the face of danger that should have overwhelmed him, silently testifies to divine power. For the reader, it is an invitation to recognize that God can spare us from the natural consequences of evil and adversity, transforming circumstances that should have destroyed us into signs of His benevolent action.

sens: Small flat object used for writing or noting something
Portable surface made of wood, wax, or similar material where letters are engraved or traced
Means of communicating in writing when one cannot speak
G4093.detail:
1. A tablet is a small, flat, portable object on which characters or signs are written. It is a simpler writing instrument than a parchment or scroll — easy to hold, practical for quick notes. In Luke 1:63, Zacharias, rendered mute by the Lord, asks for a tablet to write the name of his forthcoming son: it is the only means of communication.
2. In the ancient world, a tablet was generally a wooden surface coated with wax, where letters were traced with a stylus (the back of the stylus erased what had just been written). It was the ancient equivalent of paper or a notepad: lightweight, reusable, inexpensive.
3. By extension, the tablet symbolizes the written word, the message entrusted to writing when spoken words are impossible. For Zacharias, mute, it becomes the instrument of divine revelation: he affirms through the engraved letters the name that the Holy Spirit has made known to him.
G4093.origine: The Greek word pinakidion is a diminutive of pinakis ("plank," "plate"). The suffix -idion expresses smallness and affection: a "small tablet." This family of words designates flat surfaces, objects that are displayed or consulted. In Hebrew, there are analogous terms for small engraved plaques (like the shofar or the scribe's writing tablet), but no direct translation of pinakidion in the Greek Old Testament.
G4093.emploi: The word pinakidion appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 1:63, during the birth of John the Baptist. Zacharias, an old man rendered mute for not believing the promise of the angel Gabriel, asks for a tablet to communicate his secret: he writes the name that God has chosen for his son. This passage shows that the tablet was an everyday object in Palestinian Jewish life in the first century, common enough to be requested spontaneously and portable enough to have on hand. Its use here emphasizes the importance of writing as a means to certify and publicly testify to a divine word.
G4093.portee: For the Christian reader, this tablet embodies the power of the divine word entrusted to writing. Zacharias cannot speak, but he can write — and this act of writing is an act of faith and obedience. It reminds us that God speaks, that His word is fulfilled, and that even human silence or powerlessness cannot block His action. Zacharias' tablet also foreshadows the role of the apostles and the Church: to fix in writing the testimony of God so that all generations may benefit from it.

sens: Dish, generally flat and shallow, used to present or serve food
Object made of wood or metal shaped flat
G4094.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a dish, a hollow and wide table utensil intended to present food. This is the most common image in the gospels: when Herodias asks for "the head of John the Baptist on a plate" (Matthew 14:8, Mark 6:25), she speaks of the ordinary vessel in which dishes were served. The plate was then an everyday object, as mundane as a glass today.
2. The word can more broadly refer to any flat object made of wood or metal — a tablet, a disk, a flat surface. In Luke 11:39, the Lord mentions "the cup and the plate" that the Pharisees clean carefully: the plate here represents the visible and external table utensils, while the inside of the one using them remains impure. The image invites reflection on the apparent emptiness of beautiful dishes on the outside, while the heart is full of greed.
G4094.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to plane" or "to flatten." In Greek, pinax originally designates a flat surface — a board or tablet — before being applied to flat dishes and other shaped objects. The family includes Greek words designating flat worked surfaces, writing boards, or table objects.
G4094.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, all in the synoptic gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke). Three of these occurrences (Matthew 14:8, 11 and Mark 6:25, 28) recount the same tragic event: the request for the head of John the Baptist on a plate. In this context, the plate is a mundane object but acquires a terrible symbolic charge: it becomes the vessel of injustice, of the death of an innocent. A fifth use appears in Luke 11:39, where Jesus criticizes the Pharisees who clean the inside and outside of the plate: here, the word evokes the tableware that is meticulously cleaned to maintain appearances, while the heart remains impure. The meaning remains concrete — it is still an object — but the significance becomes moral and spiritual.
G4094.portee: This word reminds us that the dishes, the mundane utensils of everyday life, can become the stage for human drama and divine judgment. For the Christian reader, it invites us to see beyond appearances: the Pharisees washed their plates but neglected their souls. It is a lesson in humility — it is not the external objects that need to be washed first, but the heart.

sens: To absorb a liquid through the mouth
To habitually consume a beverage
To receive a drink from someone or something
To absorb or soak in (figuratively)
To participate in a destiny or spiritual reality (metaphorical sense)
G4095.detail:
1. It is the action of bringing a liquid to one's mouth and swallowing it: to drink water, wine, etc. Matthew 27:34 shows Jesus tasting the wine mixed with gall that is offered to him but refusing to drink it.

2. When the verb describes a habit, it refers to the regular consumption of beverages. Luke 1:15 speaks of John the Baptist who will drink neither wine nor strong drink in his life.

3. Often it is specified where the drink comes from: "to drink from" a well, "to drink at" a spring, "to drink from" someone's hand. In John 4:7-14, Jesus asks the Samaritan woman for a drink, and the water becomes the image of eternal life.

4. Figuratively, the earth "drinks" the rain that penetrates and enriches it (Hebrews 6:7): this is the image of absorption.

5. In the spiritual context, especially in John, "to drink the blood of the Son of Man" (John 6:53) means to receive and integrate the life that Christ offers through his sacrifice — not in a literal sense, but as a living participation in his work of salvation. Similarly, "to drink the cup" (Matthew 26:39-42) means to accept the destiny or trial that God gives.
G4095.origine: The Greek verb πίνω (pinō) comes from an ancient root that imitates the sound of the action. In the Greek Bible (Septuagint), it regularly translates the Hebrew שָׁתָה (shatah), which has exactly the same meaning. The word has been used since the earliest texts of Greek and gradually enriches itself with figurative meanings: drinking becomes a strong biblical image to signify receiving or participating in a spiritual reality.
G4095.emploi: The verb "to drink" appears 66 times in the Greek New Testament. It is found everywhere: in the Gospels, it first denotes the common action of drinking (Luke 5:33, John 4:7), then habitual consumption (Luke 1:15), and finally the offering of drink or sharing (Matthew 26:27-29 at the Last Supper). In Paul, the word enriches: drinking becomes participation, communion, received inheritance (1 Corinthians 10:4, 21). Revelation uses it for God's judgment, as in the cup of his wrath (Revelation 14:10). Jesus uses the verb in a spiritual and unusual way: drinking his blood means receiving salvation (John 6:53-56).
G4095.portee: For the believer, this word opens two major teachings: first, daily trust — Jesus invites us not to worry about what we will drink and eat, for our Father knows what we need (Matthew 6:25). Secondly, it reveals how we receive salvation: not as a concept, but as something we deeply integrate, that we "drink" — a living exchange with Christ through his sacrifice and presence. Drinking becomes the biblical symbol of active acceptance and intimate participation.

sens: Fatty substance from the body or meat
Material abundance and prosperity
Spiritual wealth and divine blessings
G4096.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to fatty matter, the fatty thickness of flesh or lard: the nourishing and rich substance found in sacrificed animals or meat.
2. It then evokes abundance and prosperity, as one would say "the fat years": the idea of a period or situation that is rich and generous, providing much.
3. In Romans 11:17, it symbolizes God's spiritual blessings: being "made a partaker of the fatness of the olive tree" means sharing the inner wealth, graces, and promises that God granted to the chosen people. The cultivated olive tree represents Israel, and its "fatness" the spiritual gifts accumulated over the centuries.
G4096.origine: The word comes from the ancient Greek πίων (pion), which means "fat," "corpulent." It has a common Indo-European root with the Latin word "pinguis" (fat). In Greek, the word always refers to the idea of rich substance and abundance. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew דֶּשֶׁן (deshen), which designates both animal fat and, figuratively, the riches of the promised land.
G4096.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 11:17. Paul uses it in an agricultural and theological comparison: he explains that believers from the nations (represented by a wild olive tree grafted in) have become partakers of the promises made to Israel (the "root and fatness of the olive tree"). Here, "fatness" does not refer to a physical substance, but rather to spiritual wealth, blessings, and privileges of the people of Israel. It is a rare, almost scholarly word that reinforces the biblical image of divine abundance.
G4096.portee: This word invites the believer to realize that in Christ, he inherits the promises and blessings accumulated by God for his people. Being "a partaker of the fatness of the olive tree" means that we taste the generosity, spiritual wealth, and love that God has always offered. It is a call to gratitude: we receive what we have not earned.

sens: To transfer a property in exchange for money
To set or estimate the price of something
To deliver someone into slavery for payment
To be dominated by, to be enslaved to
G4097.detail:
1. To exchange a property for money: this is the simplest and most common meaning. The merchant of pearls in Matthew 13:46 sells all he has to buy one. The early Christians in Acts 2:45 sold their possessions to share among all.
2. To express the market value, the price: when one says "to sell dearly," one states what something is worth. The nard in Matthew 26:9 could have been sold for a very high price.
3. To deliver a person into slavery: this is a dark usage of the word, where the insolvent servant of Matthew 18:25 is sold, he and his family, to repay his debt.
4. Figuratively, to be sold to something means to be completely submissive to it, to be its slave: Paul says in Romans 7:14 that he is sold to sin, dominated by it despite his good intentions.
G4097.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that means exchange and commercial transaction. In the Greek Old Testament, it renders the Hebrew verb "makhar," which similarly denotes the act of selling. This word belonged to the vocabulary of the market and daily economic life, hence its metaphorical use to express enslavement.
G4097.emploi: The verb "to sell" appears nine times in the New Testament. Matthew and Mark place it in the story of the precious nard poured on Jesus, where the disciples are indignant that it was not sold for money to be given to the poor (Matthew 26:9, Mark 14:5). John reports the same event (John 12:5). Matthew also uses it for the pearl of great price (Matthew 13:46) and for the servant sold into slavery (Matthew 18:25). Acts shows it in the present: the early Christians were continually selling their goods (Acts 2:45, 4:34, 5:4). Romans 7:14 elevates the word to a moral and spiritual sense: the apostle describes himself as "sold to sin," a slave to a power that oppresses him. The word thus oscillates between concrete economic meaning and moral or spiritual servitude.
G4097.portee: This word invites the Christian to reflect on his priorities and attachments. The precious pearl of Matthew 13:46 reminds us that the Kingdom of God is worth sacrificing everything else. The sharing of goods in Acts shows the generosity of the new heart. And Paul's confession in Romans 7:14 — "sold to sin" — speaks to the heart of anyone struggling against evil: before Jesus, man is a slave, powerless; only Christ can redeem and free him.

sens: To descend or be projected downward, toward the ground or into a place
To fall to the ground, collapse or be overturned
To kneel, to throw oneself at someone's feet in a sign of respect or supplication
To be destroyed, ruined, annihilated
To lose firmness, to fail, to succumb
To be fulfilled, to come to pass
G4098.detail:
1. To fall primarily means to descend or be projected downward: a seed falls to the ground (Luke 8:5), stars fall from the sky (Revelation 6:13), a bird falls on the path (Matthew 10:29). It is the quintessential physical movement.
2. The fall can be brutal and destructive: a house that falls collapses (Matthew 7:25), a man falls and dies (Acts 5:5). It is a violent or sudden event.
3. However, to fall can also be voluntary and respectful: to kneel at someone's feet (John 11:32), to throw oneself on the ground in supplication (Matthew 18:29) or in worship (Matthew 2:11). It is the humble attitude of one who recognizes the greatness of another.
4. To fall takes on a figurative meaning when it involves moral or spiritual ruin: a wall falls at God's judgment (Hebrews 11:30), a number or lot "falls" in casting lots (Acts 1:26), one "falls" under judgment (James 5:12).
5. To fall also means to fail or yield: not to fall into sin (1 Corinthians 10:12), not to fall like the Israelites who sinned (Hebrews 3:17). It is to lose moral or spiritual stability.
6. Finally, in prophecies, "to fall" means to be fulfilled or realized: not a jot of the Law will fall without being fulfilled (Luke 16:17). It is the idea of a word coming to pass.
G4098.origine: The Greek word πίπτω comes from an ancient root expressing downward movement. In Hebrew, it primarily translates to נָפַל (nafal). This root first evokes simple physical falling, but it enriches itself with moral and theological significance: to fall is not only to descend but also to lose one's place, status, or integrity. The word has many compounds in Greek (ἀπο-πίπτω, ἐκ-πίπτω, κατα-πίπτω) that nuance the idea according to the direction or intensity of the fall.
G4098.emploi: The verb πίπτω is used about 85 times in the New Testament. It appears in all four Gospels to describe concrete falls (seeds in the parable of the sower, Matthew 13:4-8) and prostrations before Jesus or God (Matthew 2:11, Revelation 4:10). In Acts and the Epistles, it often denotes spiritual ruin or the fulfillment of divine judgments. In Paul, it relates to temptation and sin: the believer risks "falling" if he thinks he is unshakeable (1 Corinthians 10:12), but he can also be lifted up by the grace of the Lord (Romans 14:4). In Revelation, it is heavily used for the fall of cosmic powers and the prostration of creatures before the throne of God. The meaning thus varies from the concrete to the figurative, from the physical to the spiritual.
G4098.portee: This word teaches the believer two essential lessons. First, human weakness: we are fragile, exposed to falling, unable to stand by our own strength — hence the importance of not boasting (1 Corinthians 10:12). Second, the right humility: to fall at the feet of Jesus or God in worship is not a shame, but an act of wisdom and respect. The sincere prostration of the heart, acknowledging our smallness and the greatness of God, is true wisdom.

sens: region of Asia Minor, corresponding to the southwest of present-day Turkey
G4099.detail: 1. Pisidia is a region of Asia Minor (present-day Turkey), located in the southwest. Paul and Barnabas pass through it during their first missionary journey: they arrive at Antioch in Pisidia via the city of Perga (Acts 13:14), and depart for Pamphylia (Acts 14:24). It is there that Paul preaches in the synagogue, and his words provoke both interest and opposition from Jews and Gentiles.
G4099.origine: Πισιδία is the Greek name for this historical region. The Pisidians form a distinct people, at the borders of Phrygia and Pamphylia. The name in Greek simply designates the territory and its inhabitants.
G4099.emploi: Pisidia is mentioned twice in the book of Acts, both times during Paul's first missionary journey. In Acts 13:14, Paul and Barnabas arrive at Antioch in Pisidia after passing through Perga; in Acts 14:24, they leave Pisidia to go to Pamphylia. These passages show the geographical itinerary of the apostolic journey through Asia Minor. Antioch in Pisidia is an important center where Paul encounters a synagogue and can preach to Jews and proselytes.
